episodes.title: If You Feel Stuck, Watch This | Zig Ziglar on Success & Environment
episodes.text:
They bring up such a good point that debt isn't just related to money. Debt relates to sensory overload, relationship debt, health debt, flexibility debt — there are several things that can be equated to debt. And when we go into debt, there is an interest that is going to be paid, and we are not getting an interest coming back to us. It is costly.

Perhaps a parable will help make the point. High on a hilltop overlooking the beautiful city of Venice, there lived an old man who was a genius. Legend had it he could answer any question anyone might ask him. Two of the local boys figured they could fool the old man, so they caught a small bird and headed for his residence. One of the boys held the little bird in his hand and asked the old man if the bird was dead or alive. Without hesitation, the old man said, "Son, if I say to you the bird is alive, you will close your hands and crush him to death. If I say the bird is dead, you will open your hands and he will fly away. You see, son, in your hands you hold the power of life and death. This I say to you without qualification and with no mental reservations whatsoever."

Welcome to the Cashflow Legends podcast with your hosts Nate, Brandon, and Brock. Remember, our insights are not direct financial advice, so consult with your financial team before making any decisions based on the topics discussed in this show.

Good morning, good morning everybody. Nate opens by noting it was a good, productive weekend — isn't it amazing how lots of things we put off, once we finally get started on them, turn out not to be that bad, like cleaning the garage. That's what they focused on the day before: clearing out space and finally seeing more of the floor.

One strategy that's been around a long time — learned through mentoring and coaching — is the brain dump: get a piece of paper and write down everything that's clogging up your brain to get it out. It's like closing tabs on a computer so your brain runs faster, because those little nagging things — walking through the garage and thinking "I need to clean that, that's bothering me, I could throw that away" — create mental drag over time.

That connects to the Chinese proverb: it's not the mountain in front of us, but the pebble in our shoe. A pebble in the shoe will aggravate you the longer you let it stay there, so being aware of that matters. Some people spend their life waiting for their circumstances to change instead of changing their circumstances.

That's a good segue back into See You at the Top by Zig Ziglar. If you don't know who Zig Ziglar is, it's worth pulling up some of his audio or finding him on YouTube and just listening for five or ten minutes to the mindset behind what he talks about. Nate and Brandon never shy away from their Christian faith, and Ziglar shared that same faith, which is part of why it resonates. With so much information out there today, you're better off picking one thing and focusing on it — pulling it in like a sponge for as long as possible — before trying to juggle 37 different sources.

One of Ziglar's early sections in the book is titled "It's in Your Hands, Son," which ties into the idea that your environment changes you, or you have the potential to change your environment. That connects to the idea of being a thermostat versus a thermometer: a thermometer just tells you the temperature, but a thermostat actually sets the temperature and sets the tone — one is passive, one is active.

Through years in business and learning from successful people in the areas of faith, family, fitness, and finances, the pattern is that those people change the temperature in the room — not in a boastful way, but in a humble, "let me help you" way. It's a noticeable trait to look for in people: do they bring value to the room, or do they just point out what's wrong with the temperature, when in reality anyone can get up and change the thermostat themselves.

That leads back to the parable of the two boys and the bird trying to trick the wise old man on the hilltop overlooking Venice — the same story about holding the power of life and death in your hands. In your hands you hold the seeds of failure or the potential for greatness. Your hands are capable, but they must be used, and used for the right thing, to reap the rewards you're capable of attaining.

There's an earlier section in the book about limiting beliefs: you've never heard anyone say a newborn was born a lawyer, a doctor, a teacher, a failure, or a success — it's always just a boy or a girl. But when people die, they're remembered as a well-known lawyer, a pastor after God's own heart who served people. The point is we have a lot of ability to control what we do with what's already in our hands.

One common misconception is the saying "it takes money to make money." There's some truth to that, but it isn't a cut-and-dried truth, because money follows value — just like the value in that bird depends on what you do with your hands, our day-to-day interactions are the same: every day is an opportunity to let that bird flourish or to crush it.

Heading into the new year, the hosts discuss what they're each leaning into. One mentions intentionality as the theme for the year — inviting accountability, including giving permission to be called out when there's a gap in the schedule, rather than filling free time with something like Netflix. Recognizing that the time God has given during the day means letting work be worship — not lightly, because everything done is an act of worship, a form of stewarding what's been put in front of you.

That brought up the movie Mr. Holland's Opus: at a high level, Mr. Holland plans to create a masterpiece but takes a teaching job to support himself while working on it. He spends decades reworking the masterpiece, and by the time he's pushed into retirement after 40-plus years, he hears a sound in the auditorium as he's leaving the building — all the students, staff, teachers, and parents he impacted are gathered, and his former musicians are now playing his masterpiece for him. The lesson: interruptions are part of the work, not something to avoid so you can get to the "real" work.

That led to a plug for a new ebook — about a 10-15 minute read — covering the three money problems (the "three M's") that everyone faces. Over eight years of doing this, the discovery has been that if you can solve those three money problems, you can turn them into a masterpiece. That's an evolution in thinking: recognizing it's all a gift, and that value created on a bigger stage almost always comes from value created on no stage at all, because you believe in what you're doing and know it helps people.

That parallels the arc of Mr. Holland's Opus — starting out just as a stepping stone to make money while working toward the "real" masterpiece. The hosts have a Monday morning meetup for fellowship, study, and accountability, where they were reminded that people get too caught up trying to over-plan and don't stay present enough with what's already in front of them. If an interruption happens, that's okay — it's a chance to practice the fruits of the spirit already indwelling.

Words matter: one host caught himself about to say "I have to" about something involving his kids, and corrected it to "I get to." That small shift in language — "I get to" instead of "I have to" — can create real power in your life, because when you say you have the privilege of doing something, you're forced to define why it's a privilege, which pushes you into gratitude. You can't be frustrated and in gratitude at the same time, just like you can't be in comparison and in gratitude at the same time — and everyone wants to be happy and winning, which comparison doesn't allow.

They also discussed a recurring practice of studying how they allot their day in 15-minute sections. Entrepreneurs aren't as different from employees as people assume — everyone has something on their schedule to do or not do, allotting time or energy, and if you don't track it, you're often doing something different than you think you are. Over a recent weekend, the challenge was to find something that would give back 10 hours a week to focus clearly on where they're going and why. That meant first getting clear on the destination, then understanding the motivation behind it.

It only took 30 seconds to make the change — not because of anything magical, but because of having done this so many times before: removing Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and Gmail — all social media connections — not because they're not valuable, but because the data shows it's a time warp that pulls away from what you actually want to accomplish with the gifts you've been given. That freed up roughly 10 hours.

The challenge to listeners: check your screen time. It's a clear indicator of where your mind goes. There are two costs to jumping into an app while trying to focus on something else: the opportunity cost of not being able to do something else at the same time, and the fact that a "quick" 30-second distraction actually takes much longer to recover from, because focus breaks and it takes real time to regain it when jumping in and out of different apps.

One tactic mentioned: going grayscale on your phone. Screens are designed with vivid colors because we're drawn to them — devices are built to keep us on them, because we are the product. Switching to grayscale removes the appeal, and suddenly the phone is just a tool again.

That connects to material from Fig and Eagle (a family accountability training program) about how debt isn't just about money — there's sensory overload debt, relationship debt, health debt, flexibility debt — and all of it carries an interest cost without an interest return. Even after deleting social media apps, there was a tendency to find another app to escape into rather than stay focused — not necessarily escaping anything bad, since life is good, but escaping from staying locked into a single task for 15, 20, 30, or 45 minutes at a time.

Every person has some kind of addiction or craving that never fully goes away — the key is finding something positive to feed it and replacing it regularly. A quote from Joe Polish (crediting Scott Donnell) came up: overworking, hustle culture, is one of the most addictive, non-substance things in today's world — arguably more addicting than many things people call addictions, and it's socially acceptable, which makes it worse. It's also the opposite of creating value: there's a statistically proven net negative after eight hours of work. Push to 9, 10, 11, 12 hours and the marginal return shrinks; go past 12 and the return actually goes negative — and that connects back to all the "debts" discussed earlier.

Closing thought: the goal is to keep bringing value to listeners on this life journey. Money will always be intertwined, but as the hosts often say, it isn't really about the money — money is just fuel for clarity, or it takes away from clarity. For anyone who feels they have a beautiful bird in their hands and isn't sure how to help it grow and take off, the hosts remain open to topic requests and ideas, not because they've figured everything out, but because they enjoy the process of figuring things out to share with others. They thanked listeners for sharing their greatest asset — their time.

episodes.title: Money Follows Value: Why Self-Worth Drives Wealth
episodes.text:
Money follows value. Said another way, the more genuinely we lean into what we're here to do, how we're here to create value, no matter where we're working or what we're working on, opportunity starts finding that value that you create. And it is not a straight line, and it's not 1 + 1 = 2 and 2 + 2 = 4 and so on. Often it's like we're eight years in, Nate, and that book and that person that we met seven years ago now is a foundational piece of all the relationships we have, because they were genuine. They were not a counterfeit, or because we were genuine and we weren't a counterfeit. And there are always two sides to everything. For everything that's genuine, there is a counterfeit. There's no way around it. We can either exert energy being genuine or energy being a counterfeit, and I'm going to call myself out. The greatest lies I tell to myself are to the counterfeit version of myself that's opposite to the genuine version that I say I want to be, once we get more efficient with the money that's flowing through our life. As long as our heart posture is correct, then once some of our needs start to be satisfied, that frees us up mentally. Now we can finally start focusing on how we can serve the people around us so that it can overflow and fill everybody. Welcome to the Cashflow Legendz podcast with your hosts Nate, Brandon, and Brock.

Remember, our insights are not direct financial advice, so consult with your financial team before making any decisions based on the topics discussed in this show.

What's going on everybody? Nate, how are you this morning, brother?

Well, man, it's a good, it's a fine Monday morning.

It is indeed. So, Nate, you had a lot of traveling going on this weekend, and we talked several times, and there was definitely some times where it was exhausting, or y'all were up late, or y'all were driving home late. But is there anything that you took away from getting away for the weekend with a lot of your family and supporting your boys and your nephew on pursuing bringing value to this world in different ways? A key takeaway maybe from the time that y'all drove down and spent time with family and watched your sons and your nephew get on stage and be recognized for putting in the work.

Well, you know, we talk about creating a life that you don't want to escape from. And yeah, it was a weekend that we took the time to go do that, but the reality is that if we wanted to, we could go during the week. And as I was kind of thinking through the experience and the weekend, one sort of prevailing thought for me was: the life that I'm creating for myself has brought so much joy and love into our family that I want my story to continue through my bloodline. I want to give my kids similar opportunities that I had, maybe not doing the exact same thing, but just living that out in front of them. And this goes back to the story of growing up in a household where my dad was a business owner and he showed up for everything. He was there. He built a life where he could spend time with his family, and watching that for many years, I remember just thinking, I want to live like that.

Nate, it just dawned on me — I've never thought about this before in all of our conversations and all of our podcast episodes we've done with Cashflow Legendz and the topics we've broached — you and I have parents that showed up. My dad worked a W-2 job and my mom was a business owner, but he worked a W-2 job for over forty years that allowed him the flexibility to prioritize family. So I think that's a great connection to know that you, and I, and Brock — we don't always say this, but we're not saying everybody's meant to be a business owner.

No, go ahead.

Well, what we are saying is that we have to choose where we're going to put our time, energy, and effort. And there is a cost to everything we do, even if it's doing nothing. So we have to first reckon with that. My dad worked forever at what I thought was a great job with great benefits, some of the best insurance you could have, and they were great providers for our family and still are. But to hear my dad rethink his thinking, as Nelson said, has been really fascinating and fun to listen to. Same with your stepdad and your mom and how they've rethought their thinking and continue to. So I think it's a good segue into today: we all have gifts that we're given, and those gifts are going to be used for genuine reasons or they're going to be counterfeit.

And there's a great story in the book See You at the Top about genuine versus counterfeit. It's about a guy named Emanuel Ninger. Late 1800s, he walks into a grocery store — almost 1900 — and he pays with a twenty-dollar bill for some turnip greens. Twenty dollars in 1887 was a lot of money, probably like handing over a hundred-plus dollars today, if not more. He hands the twenty over, and this is a guy known in the community as an artist, somebody good at what he does. The young lady who takes his money notices a little smudge of ink on her fingers and doesn't think much of it at first. Mr. Ninger leaves, and as she keeps thinking on it, she realizes there has to be a reason there's ink on her hand. So she begins to wonder if maybe she needs to report it to the police to see if he gave her a counterfeit bill, since there's no other reason she'd have ink on her hand from a genuine bill. She wrestles with it for a while, finally calls the police. They go to Emanuel Ninger's house, and not only do they find counterfeit material in the attic where he's been making twenty-dollar bills, they find one he's working on right then — and he was such a talented artist that he was doing this entirely by hand. Just by bad luck, her hands happened to be wet from something she'd been doing, and hadn't completely dried off, which made the ink leak. He's arrested — counterfeiting money is a no-no in any world — but there were three portraits up in that attic that he had painted. When he went to prison, those three portraits sold for sixteen thousand dollars total. It took him almost the exact same amount of time to paint a portrait with his gifts as it did to paint a counterfeit twenty-dollar bill.

If we could share any encouragement with anyone, wherever their feet are, wherever the Lord's put them to bring value — they're there for a reason, but they get to choose whether they're going to create something genuine or something counterfeit.

And let's throw ourselves under the bus, Nate — there have been times when I've been in certain places, working certain jobs, where I haven't brought my most genuine effort because I was so focused on this isn't the job I want, or this isn't where I want to go, or I'm not valued, or I'm mistreated, and the list goes on. So we're not throwing rocks at anybody — we're just saying we were created to create genuine value in all things we do, and the amount of effort we put in is going to either create genuine value or counterfeit value. But we are going to be affected by it either way. Would you agree?

Yeah, for sure. And one of the points that Zig makes in this story is that oftentimes the greatest thief in our life is ourselves — not really recognizing our true value, our true worth, what our time is worth, all that stuff. And it goes back to something we talk about often: you and I have a group of men we pour into each week, and one of the values of having trusted relationships around you is for people to call things up in you, to point out your worth, to point out things about you that you may not see in yourself. And I would venture to guess no one in Emanuel's life had ever come alongside him and said, "These portraits are amazing."

Yeah, it's a great point, Nate. Encouragement in our life, with people we trust, allows counterfeit things that are going on to be called out quickly, because you and I believe this strongly — we believe it's scriptural — living life on your own without fellowship and accountability is not what we're called to do as believers. I'm certain of that. I'm not certain of a whole lot, but I'm certain we are not meant to lock ourselves in the attic painting twenty-dollar counterfeit bills instead of getting out there and showing everybody what God's created through us to glorify him.

Is it wild to you, Nate, that the same amount of energy put into painting a counterfeit bill also went into creating a masterpiece? In any capacity, one thing that comes to mind for me is: when we're presented with information in our life about whatever circumstances, it takes energy to create a negative story attached to that information, and it also takes energy to create a positive story attached to that circumstance. So where is your energy best spent — creating a negative story for yourself, or creating a positive story? Because until you have more information, both of those stories are made up. So where is the highest value use of that energy going to be spent?

Nate, when I think about counterfeit, I think about comparison. So many times in the social media world — we talk about this often — there's a balance between sharing all the things we've learned and being humble in sharing that, while also being aware that we should see social media for what it is. If we don't know the person on the other side of that screen well, if we haven't had in-depth conversations with them, we need to assume with grace and understanding and mercy that they're probably showing the best version of themselves and sharing the best version of that. We have to show up with humility, because the breath we have, the opportunities we have, the relationships, the challenges, the tests — those are all for one thing: to give God the glory and to love others as we love ourselves.

Yeah, and we try to be the best example we can be, for our family first, then our friends and acquaintances. We put ourselves out there, but we're not perfect. We don't have it all figured out. So when we're sharing good information, we're also talking to ourselves about it. Just this past week there was a situation — I won't go into detail — where my wife found out something, and her next response was an assumption about that information, whereas when I heard the same thing, I did not automatically assume something else, and then we found out more information and it wasn't actually the thing we thought it was. So where I could have spent some energy going into that same place she did, I kept it high level, and my immediate response in my head was: God's already got this figured out. Now, I'd love to say I treat everything in my life that exact same way every single time, but in that moment I did — I just said God's already got it figured out, so I didn't have to spend that negative energy.

Yeah, and before we hit record we were talking about — I wrote this down as we were studying through a book — and let me clarify for anybody catching the middle of this: when we're talking about negative and positive energy, that is not new-age language or anything like that; you have to understand the context of what we're talking about. Yeah, absolutely, really where our mind is going, that's our energy — how we think about it, what we're consuming, what our thoughts are. But we were talking about this this morning: one of the most powerful words I've learned to use over the last several years, from all the coaching and teaching we've had and invested in, is the word "maybe." Maybe we don't know this, or maybe we don't understand that, or maybe they're dealing with something we don't understand. Every time a moment occurs, my wife Leah is way better at this than me — she doesn't assume anything other than maybe this or maybe that, and there's grace given. Whereas back in my principal days, my assumption was always there was no maybe or grace — it was like they're out to hurt me or ruin something about me. And the reality is the only way we can really understand someone genuinely is to spend time with them or with that situation. So when we think about Emanuel Ninger, maybe he never had anybody share his artwork and say, "You are talented, man." Maybe he never shared it with anybody, and there might be a reason that's the case.

In the world we're in with money, it's never about the money first — it's always about whether you're genuinely working toward the life you're called to live, and whether your dollars are pushing, magnifying, and accelerating that life and purpose genuinely. On the flip side, we're guilty of this too — the counterfeit version is the keeping-up-with-the-Joneses that we're always aware of. I still battle it, because it really feels good to have something you think everybody else sees and thinks is cool. There's nothing wrong with that, but there is if it supersedes anything else and it's not genuinely who we are. So what would be your thoughts on how to turn counterfeit failures into genuine wins?

Well, first, when you said that about keeping up with the Joneses — here's a framework you can use to make sure your decision-making is in alignment with your values. When you see something you'd want to purchase that might be considered a status symbol to some, ask yourself: if no one ever knew I had this, would I still want it? Because chasing status is a counterfeit game in and of itself. Almost anybody you talk to — we were talking about this a couple weeks ago in our Sunday morning Bible study at church — the newness of getting something, that feeling you're chasing and finally get, usually only lasts a couple weeks and then it's gone. So how much did you work to get that thing? How much energy did you spend in your mind thinking about it, only to find out the feeling of actually getting it was very fleeting?

Yeah, let's think about this from a perspective of time. This reminds me of one of my favorite baseball stories — a reliever in the minor leagues who normally worked right after the starter, either the gap filler to get to the closer, or the cleanup guy when they were already losing or winning by a lot. He comes into his manager and says, "Hey, Skip, I really think I'm ready to be the eighth or ninth inning guy." And the skipper, as deadpan as he could be, looks at him and says, "I really think when you start pitching like it in the innings you already pitch, you may be the eighth or ninth inning guy." So how many times have we wanted something else when we weren't even being good stewards of what we already genuinely had? And how many times do we see that when we're having conversations with couples or business owners who say they want all these things with money, but we've not gotten down to the foundation of what we genuinely want, because we're so in the day-to-day that we can't see straight?

Yeah, it reminds me of something Jim Rohn said — and I don't want anybody to misunderstand where I'm going with this — he said, "Become a millionaire so that when the money comes, you get to keep it and you know what to do with it." The idea behind that is: prepare yourself mentally, emotionally, spiritually for the things you want, so that when they actually show up in your life, you're ready for them. But really the overall theme is: make sure you're investing in your growth. There's two words that go together as we're sitting here thinking about this, thinking about our own journey so far: the more grounded we are in who we are and what we stand for and what we're here for, the more genuine we can be — the greater capacity we have to be genuine — because we know that everything on this side of eternity that's man-made, possession-wise or material-wise, is fleeting.

So anybody listening or watching this, thinking, "How does this have to do with what Nate and Brandon do with money? How does this have anything to do with what Brock teaches about working with successful business owners, and our podcast, Cashflow Legendz?" It has everything to do with it. One of the greatest things we have the opportunity to do with the genuine gifts God's given us is to share that as often as possible. Because when you take a husband and a wife who are on the same page about how money is fueling their purpose — for their family, their financial well-being, their fitness, their faith, their future — when they're on the same page and working to stay on the same page, there is nothing better to experience than watching that happen. And nowhere in there did I say anything about how many zeros are in your paycheck, or how much money you made. It was alignment, and being aware of how husband and wife, or business partner and business partner, work together, because life does this — it's a roller coaster. It doesn't do a flat line for very long; there's going to be a deep, fast, stomach-turning drop at some point. So when we say that what we teach about becoming your own banker and the infinite banking concept is just a way to take what you're already doing and create more certainty, liquidity, peace of mind, and protection — we're not trying to convince people to do something dramatically different, other than how you think about how money moves through your life. But none of that matters unless you know why you want it to move through your life a certain way.

Yeah — Saturday morning, where we were staying, there was a coffee shop right around the corner, so I walked down and got coffee and started visiting with the guy running the shop that morning. I don't think it was his shop, but I think he was working there and going to school too. And as we'd been visiting for a while, I told him, "Hey, if you ever feel like you need more peace of mind in your life, maybe we should connect more." And he said, "Man, I'm drowning in student loan debt right now." I said, "Well, that's one of the things we can help you with," and his eyes kind of lit up a little bit. Most people, until they really lean in and start having conversations with us, they have it like there's a window with a set of blinds — you can peek through, but how much can you really see just peeking through the blinds? Your peripheral is cut off; you only see a small amount of perspective in the grand scheme of things. And I know for a fact, because we've been doing this long enough, that there have been people peeking through the blinds at us, so to speak — friends and family who think they know what's going on and what we do, but they're not 100% sure. Some of them are okay just remaining in skepticism, and some are fighting their pride to reach out, and the only reason we can say that with confidence is because we've been doing this long enough — we've seen those moments where people go, "All right, I've been listening to y'all long enough, I've got to know what's going on."

And tied to this idea that money follows value: the more genuinely we lean into what we're here to do, how we're here to create value, no matter where we're working, opportunity starts finding that value we create. It's not a straight line, and it's not 1+1=2 and 2+2=4. Often it's like we're eight years in, and that book, and that person we met seven years ago, is now a foundational piece of all the relationships we have, because they were genuine, and we were genuine, not a counterfeit. And there are always two sides to everything — for everything genuine, there is a counterfeit. We can either exert energy being genuine, or energy being a counterfeit. And I'm going to call myself out — the greatest lies I tell myself are to the counterfeit version of myself, opposite to the genuine version I say I want to be. Now, we've learned that we can stay there and get beat up in the mental negative ping-pong, or we can be proud of being aware of that and go, "Okay, God's mercies are new every day. There's nothing that's a surprise to him. Where can I be better today, for him to get the glory, and for me to love others like he loves me?" That's it. You have made me a better thinker creatively, because I'll take an hour to say something and you'll say the same thing in three words, and I want to be better at that — I get around people who do things differently than I do but have the same genuine values.

This mindset is available to anybody who is willing to invest in themselves and get real clear on what the most genuine version of themselves is. And when we really start peeling back the layers of what is the genuine version of ourselves we want to be pursuing, there's going to be a lot of friction, a lot of pain — not necessarily physically, but spiritually, emotionally, socially. Somebody told me the other day, "These mindsets that are not good for us keep finding us." And I asked, "Why do you think that is?" We didn't get a whole lot of time to discuss it, but if we dove into it, it would potentially be because of how people view us, how they see us interact with others, how they see us carry ourselves — because birds of a feather do flock together. How many times have you been asked, "How do you get in conversations like this with people across the United States?" I hear it pretty often — how do you get around people who are talking about this? If you really think about where that genuinely started for us, where did we start opening up the door? It's all blessings. Accountability is where it all started — accountability, and then a curiosity that wouldn't stop for both of us. And the only way true accountability can occur is for us to be genuinely pursuing a genuine version of ourselves. So what is a genuine version of myself? It's that person inside that I know God created me to be for his kingdom and his glory, that I've got to do a whole lot of daily work and leaning into him for it to come out, because on my own it's a wreck. You'll hear some people say it this way: I just felt like I was made for more. And we're not talking about woo energy or naming and claiming or prosperity gospel, but if we believe we're created by the creator of the heavens and the earth, how could we deny that we're all created for something amazing for his kingdom? Because that's the most amazing thing there could be.

So what would be your challenge, your charge, your call to action for anybody listening or watching this later, in regard to being genuine in general — whether we like it or not, money flows through our life like oxygen and blood flow, and a genuine relationship with it will be one of the most important things we could ever do. What would be your call to action?

We want this for people who want this, because we know what it's done for us personally, and we also know what it's done for the people we get to work with all over the country. We get to see really cool stories, families growing in peace and love. You can't separate money from any of it — going back to something Zig said, money's like oxygen, you've got to have it. We're not obsessed with money, but we're not oblivious to it either — we've got to have it for food, for shelter. But the cool thing is, once we get more efficient with the money flowing through our life, as long as our heart posture is correct, once some of our needs start to be satisfied, that frees us up mentally, and now we can finally start focusing on how we can serve the people around us — filling our own cup up so it can overflow and fill everybody else. There are resources we give away freely — I posted this in the comments a little while ago, our entire thirty-video series on infinite banking, which you can get absolutely free. Go to unlimitedlifeconcepts.com, infinite bites, and that's where you can get access to all thirty videos. There's no obligation once you watch those videos to do anything with it, but what we've found is that people who lean in and start learning the truth becomes very powerful for someone, and as people watch those videos or read some of the things we recommend, action starts to take place, and transformation starts to take place. No matter how you dice it, if something's going to change, something has to change. That sounds silly and simple, but it's true. So a good way to reverse-engineer this: if you are happy, content, at peace, confident, and clear that your income-earning potential, whatever job you work, is providing the opportunity to live life on purpose the way you feel called to, then we're not a fit. If there's any hesitation, the only thing it's going to cost you is your willingness to lean into your learning — genuinely leaning into your learning and your capabilities. Buying a book that's twenty dollars called Becoming Your Own Banker, reading it, and recognizing that the only way we grow is to get real clear on where we're going and then how we're going to grow to get there. It is not a straight line.

We became accountable to each other first — it strengthened our accountability, and how God looks at iron sharpening iron. Then we started reading — and this is not to brag, because I didn't consume but about 10% of it — but we probably read over sixty books that first year. What it did is engage the brain: if you're going to be different than you are, you have to do something different. That led to us finding guys who taught becoming your own banker and infinite banking, who knew Nelson Nash personally, who knew his message, who lived IBC and Becoming Your Own Banker. And we want to share that with everyone who wants to help themselves learn something new. Here's the cool thing — as long as you get clarity on why this is or isn't for you, you will learn something if you lean into it. Because yes, we're experts in whole life insurance and how to use it for the process of banking, but we also have relationships and tax mitigation strategies and bookkeeping and protecting your income with disability insurance, and the list goes on and on, because we keep leaning in to being genuine stewards of the information and how it's genuinely been shared and coached to us. That is ongoing — it doesn't stop when we stop hitting record here. That's what we do during our air-quote work week, every week: how can we bring more value to people who need to understand this, or want to understand this, and how can we make the entry easy enough, but with enough friction that they realize this is different — we're not going to hand you something and take care of it for you; you're going to have to know why it matters to you.

So, why don't you give a little update on what you just posted in the links and what we've got coming up this coming Saturday — not this Saturday, next Saturday, my bad. So, January 31st, on Saturday from 9 to 12, we are doing our Pizza and Perspective local meetup in Marshall, Texas, where you can come hang out with us, eat some great food, get around our community, some of our awesome members who will be there, get around people who have been practicing this for a number of years, and get your questions answered. I remember getting feedback from one of our members after the very first event he went to — he said, "Man, this helped me so much because I realized I'm not doing this by myself." Sometimes when you're practicing IBC, it can feel lonely, because you're not able to have the same conversations with people that you get to have with us, so it starts to feel like you're just out here doing this thing on your own. Then you get around other people who have been doing it too, and you're like, okay, all right — we like to call that getting close to the fire, staying close to the fire. One of the beautiful things about Pizza and Perspective — this is our sixth, seventh, eighth one — we hope to embody and represent how we've been mentored, how we've been coached, how Nelson Nash's message through the workbook Becoming Your Own Banker, and through our mentors Mike Ever and Chris Bay, and through the community as a whole, has poured into us to realize that we can't drag you into this. As Mayor Joe says, if we drag you in, we've got to drag you around. And that's true for anything — if you want to be exceptional at something, you have to be willing to work harder than the people introducing you to the thing. So you're going to hear things like "leaders are readers," and "who do you surround yourself with to challenge your thinking, who can call you up when you are being a counterfeit version of the genuine version you said you wanted to be?" One of the things I love to hear as feedback from members, people we get to spend a lot of time with, is not only have you helped me create my IBC system, but you have encouraged me to continue to grow and be better. I love hearing that, because the goal in all of this is just to lift people up, and like you said earlier, it really ain't about the money — the money is really just a necessary part of the process, because it's part of everything we do. But this is so much more about relationships and figuring out how we can bring value to someone.

So we'll finish with this: I was doing a little bit of math yesterday, and if you hear us talking about whole life insurance and premiums, and you have any negative connotation in your mind about what those things mean, I cannot encourage you enough to come to a Pizza and Perspective, message us at cashflowlegends.com, watch the Infinite Bites, do something that pushes you forward to think about your thinking — which was one of Nelson's principles, rethink your thinking — because small, consistent actions over long periods of time create a compound effect that sometimes we don't realize until we stop and do the math. So maybe come join our Pizza and Perspective, and Nate and I'll share with you inside of our families how many premiums we've paid, how much cash value that's created to control the banking function, and just as importantly, how much death benefit that has protected for our estate that we'll pass on to the next generation, for the heritage we are practicing leaving with our children and grandchildren that we don't have yet. If any of that interests you, message us, check in — you may not regret it, you'll appreciate this. Just had one of our members send me a text — he's wanting to come, wants to know if he can bring his 15-year-old son. I said, "Yes, bring him. Absolutely." Here's a last little encourager for parents: even if you don't have your money in order, it will take somebody else's view outside the jar to help you read your label. Don't feel bad about that — that is normal. We have to have that in our life, mentors reading our jar from outside the label, because they're not emotionally attached, so we won't feel attacked. This is just a conversation we have with everybody. One of the greatest gifts we can give to our children is to teach them that money is just a tool, and how to use it in a way that perpetuates your family heritage, your family purpose, your family passions, in a way that continues even when you and I are not here. Because at the end of the day, when we pass away, we're with Jesus — we're not worried about nothing anymore. That's the best way my brain can process it. But there still is work to be done on this earth, and whether we like it or not, money fuels purpose, money fuels good, money fuels evil. So we have to reckon with that.

You got anything else?

It's a good place to end. Appreciate everybody joining on this, listening later, the likes, the subscribes, the follows on Facebook and all the places that host Cashflow Legendz on the podcast. We're just grateful that you share your time with us. We do not take that lightly. Have a blessed day.

episodes.title: What Lens Are You Looking Through?
episodes.text:
Becoming your own banker is a mindset, a behavior, a lifestyle — not something mystic or magical. It's simply a matter of learning some truths about money, the different "locations" money can go, the rules of those locations, and what you can and can't do within those rules. Nate and Brandon open by noting how often people tell them, "You're asking questions no one has ever asked me," and how big a responsibility that is. Welcome to the Cash Flow Legends podcast with hosts Nate, Brandon, and Brock — this show is not direct financial advice, so consult your financial team before making decisions based on the topics discussed.

Nate kicks off the topic with an analogy he'd posted: putting on a new pair of glasses feels off at first, but then everything gets sharper — the same thing happens when someone finally sees money through the correct lens and the right philosophy. Their income doesn't necessarily change, their effort doesn't necessarily change, but once the lens is correct, their financial world opens up and the truth can't be unseen. Nate jokes they aren't eye doctors, but they do help people correct their financial vision — hence the question, "What lens are you looking through?"

Brandon builds on this: people often don't realize their "eyesight" is out of adjustment until they slow down enough to try another lens. They can't force anyone to swap their glasses, but they can create the willingness to ask, "What would it look like through a different lens?" Nate adds that most people are just one in-depth question away from realizing they've already felt or experienced something they never had language for. Their role isn't to tell people what to do — it's to introduce information, connect dots based on the energy and effort someone is already putting in, and let them decide if they want a new prescription.

They discuss letting people "try on a pair" of glasses through free resources, including their new ebook at 3mpbook.com, which covers the three money problems everyone faces at some level. Brandon shares that after sending the ebook to someone, the person read it and immediately asked what the next step was — proof that sharing information only works if the person chooses to act on it. After eight years of practicing becoming your own banker, they've found that most people's hesitation to try something different comes down to not having anyone around them consistently advocating for their financial decisions or helping them get clear on what matters most.

Brandon shares that people have told him he asks questions no one else has, and pushes them to think about things they've never considered — a huge honor and responsibility. One prospect asked if Brandon was going to "scold" him the way another advisor had; Brandon said no, and that he's never told anyone to sell their car and eat rice and beans. Their motto, "live different, live unlimited," reflects that they're swimming upstream compared to conventional financial advice.

Nate emphasizes that just because something has been said loudly and consistently with a lot of marketing behind it doesn't make it true — most people repeating conventional wisdom (like "cash is king" or "debt payoff is the only way") genuinely believe it because that's what they were taught, not because they're being deceptive. Brock and Nate share the "cash versus finance" visual: if you save $500/month for ten months to buy something for $5,000 in cash, the balance grows and then disappears the moment you spend it. If you finance that same $5,000 purchase, you make payments to someone else over that same time period. Either way, you're on a "race back to zero." The insight isn't about which method is objectively better — cash gives you control over saving and access, while financing gives you the item sooner — but recognizing that both leave you starting over at zero.

The biggest "aha" moment, according to Nate, is when someone realizes that a process they'd had little control over — money flowing in and out of their life — is something they can actually take control of. When people first hear about "borrowing" within their own banking system, the early misconception is "I don't want to owe anybody anything" — but nobody has experienced owing a debt to themselves, where they control the environment of the loan. The ability to borrow money and also control when and how it flows back into the system is, in their view, deeply freeing.

Brock offers a practical exercise: list your top five automatic monthly payments that go to someone else — bills you've numbed yourself to because they're automated. Now imagine if one, two, or three of those dollar flows came back to a place you could use again. This isn't about rates of return; it's about control and certainty. For people trying to escape bad debt, credit cards, or student loans, the reason they "can't get ahead" is usually that the dollar keeps going back to zero, or an unexpected expense resets everything. Nate and Brock stress that they didn't invent any of these ideas themselves — they learned them by paying for coaching, reading, attending events, and getting into rooms with people who think this way.

They rarely see a true income-earning problem; almost always it's a cash flow system problem, sometimes tied to spending habits. Nate and Brock describe themselves as "two knuckleheads from Aledo, Texas" who don't fit neatly into the financial industry box — they teach the use of whole life insurance and insurability, but what they're really in is the peace-of-mind business. Their ideal client is someone willing to try on a different set of "prescriptions" and put in the work to learn.

They close with a plug for their in-person event, "Pizza and Perspective," held at a workshop space in downtown Marshall, Texas, hosted by the owners of Joe Pine. It's an intentionally small, personal gathering (15–25 people) with free food and conversation about becoming your own banker, framed as a no-pressure environment — "let us prove to you if you're willing to do the work." They mention resources at 3mpbook.com as an overview of their mindset and process, and clarify a common misconception: practicing becoming your own banker isn't an "or" relative to other financial strategies — it's an "and" that makes whatever else you're doing more stable and consistent, referencing Caleb Guilliams' book The And Asset. They sign off encouraging viewers to reach out via Facebook Messenger or their website if they want to take the next step.

episodes.title: I Can Get a Higher Rate of Return? Cashflow Legendz
episodes.text:
There's a delay in time while getting the banking system established. This is not get-rich-quick, not about how fast you can get cash in and pull cash out. Can that happen? Yes, but only if you know why you're doing it and how it's going to make what you're already doing better — that's where coaching comes in: if you do this, this occurs; if you do this, that occurs. Are you thinking one, two, three, five years into the future? Most people are building for retirement income primarily from the stock market — if you're pulling money out during a market decline, you risk running out of money too early, called sequence of returns risk. You have to be prepared to withstand down years with buffer years or a volatility buffer so portfolios can recover.

Welcome to the Cash Flow Legends podcast with your hosts Nate, Brandon, and Brock. Remember, our insights are not direct financial advice, so consult with your financial team before making any decisions based on the topics discussed in this show.

Recording during wild winter weather across the country — East Texas got freezing rain and shut down completely (kids out of school all week), while Brock's area in Tennessee had over 230,000 people without power at one point. Brock's brother-in-law and his fiancée got stuck at home because fallen trees and power lines blocked the road; it was eerily quiet with occasional sounds of trees falling and transformers blowing.

Brandon and his wife talked that morning about having a plan for when things don't go according to plan — East Texas isn't equipped or budgeted for this kind of weather since it happens somewhat randomly (though usually January to late February), and missing multiple days of school is rare over his lifetime there. This ties into today's topic: Nelson's Becoming Your Own Banker, pages 69-70, "But I can get a higher rate of return." Getting a higher rate of return sounds great until unexpected weather hits and the power lines freeze.

Nate's generator analogy: people don't buy generators because they know the power will go out tomorrow, but nobody regrets having one when they need it — there's always a chance something could go wrong, and every time the generator kicks in, people are grateful for the decision. Brandon relays visiting his pastor, who said there's real peace of mind in knowing his family is protected and warm when the generator kicks on. People have a natural tendency to assume things will go smoothly — no frozen power lines, no fallen trees, no burst pipes — believing it just won't happen to them.

Brock connects this to Michael Phelps, who spoke at an event Brock attended: Phelps visualized his success but also visualized everything that could go wrong — in 2008 his goggles filled with water during a gold medal race and he swam essentially blind, but because he'd mentally rehearsed things going wrong, he was prepared when it happened. No financial plan is perfect or works out 100% of the time. Brock also references Chris Jarvis (an advisor to people with massive wealth) and mentor Justin Donald discussing how no plan works out exactly as planned — you have to plan for the unexpected. The problem in financial life is you often can't get the "generator" when you need it — you have to have it beforehand. This ties to sequence of returns risk: if you're pulling retirement income from a declining stock market, you risk running out of money too early, requiring buffer years or a volatility buffer to let portfolios recover.

Brandon recalls "Snowmageddon" in 2020 driving back from Broken Bow — some states/counties were far better prepared for bad weather because they'd budgeted and planned for it as a recurring event, while family members without four-wheel drive got stranded and Brandon's family became "four-wheel drive chauffeurs." Having a four-wheel drive isn't important in East Texas most of the time, until you need it. At 65 or 70, deciding to shift life seasons, you can't just grab "20 years of market recovery" off a shelf like a generator from Home Depot — you're left riding out what you have or doing something you wish you didn't have to do.

Nate's bucket visual for sequence of returns risk: three buckets, one with a single pinhole leak, one with two, one with three — the goal is to keep water in the buckets by managing which bucket you draw from and how fast, avoiding drawing more from a bucket that's already leaking faster.

Brock shares insight from a mentor and monster producer in the industry (68 years old) about retirement and aging: as you age, there are things you want to do more of — travel, volunteer at church, attend conferences — not necessarily retire to a beach and never work, but do things without the worry of needing income from them. The other side: this mentor has double-digit numbers of friends who didn't get to choose when they retired because of dementia or similar conditions — life chooses for you. The key is having a retirement income or distribution plan that removes the fear of running out of money regardless of how or when retirement happens.

Connecting Nelson's "I can get a higher rate of return" chapter to unforeseen weather: rate of return means nothing if it's not creating freedom of choice and the ability to change as you age. Brock's example: wanting to volunteer at church without needing to be paid, because assets already generate enough income, and having enough life insurance to ensure loved ones are "replenished" or "reimbursed" upon "graduating" (Nelson's term for death). What Nate values now, reading these two pages compared to eight years ago, ties into coaching from Brock's dad Trent and others: being aware of what's going on and knowing what to do about it while things are going well. Brandon didn't like the feeling of being without power for one to two weeks last year, or not being able to get to a gas station without four-wheel drive, or being unable to reach loved ones across the county — those feelings exist at every age but hit differently in retirement years.

Rate of return is often a comparison game that doesn't tell the full story — talking with clients in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin about extreme cold made Brandon realize comparisons don't capture reality. When you control the banking function and are the owner in that environment, there's a level of profitability others may not experience, plus internal policy growth that isn't reported to or taxed by the IRS.

Nelson's key line: comparing getting a rate of return traditionally versus borrowing against your policy, "in case B, we're forgetting that we are the owner in the banking process" — and the principle applies to any investment: there's no way to get a higher rate of return by ignoring the banking process. There's a delay in time while establishing the banking system — this isn't about get-rich-quick, but knowing why and how, and thinking multiple years ahead.

Brock's approach, borrowed by Brandon: work backwards from the worst case — being 68 and no longer able to work or think straight — and ask, what do you want to be able to say for sure happened? This applies at every age (Brock in his 20s, Nate and Brandon in their 40s, their parents in their 60s-70s, grandparents in their 80s) — it's a normal conversation, but people act like it won't happen to them. The goal: being able to say that whether you're a "vegetable," fully active, or no longer here, your family's financial life isn't negatively impacted, letting them carry on the heritage instilled in them.

The real question about seeking a higher rate of return: does it move you toward what matters most to you? Nate and Brock ask tough questions partly to vet whether they're a good fit for someone, since if you don't want to be asked hard questions, they probably can't help you. Brandon shares a personal story: Brock held him accountable on completing his will and trust documentation (already delayed despite Brandon teaching this daily) by asking what consequence he'd face if he missed the deadline. Brandon proposed a $500 donation to a charity of Brock's choice; Brock instead had him pick the last place he'd want to send money — Brandon chose Planned Parenthood, given his strong feelings against it — and the task got done before the deadline, with real relief afterward. The lesson: people justify avoiding necessary tasks, and having someone in your life who'll ask bold, blunt questions while things are going well is valuable, versus having that same conversation after something bad has already happened.

Discussion on how Nate probes someone bragging about a great rate of return (e.g., a 35-year-old maxing their 401k match): is that rate of return sustainable, or did they just hit a good stretch in the market? Garrett has pointed out that someone consistently getting 12% would eventually have more money than the Federal Reserve. Nate mentions a client who saved a lot of money, went to a financial advisor, and got a plan that didn't give him peace of mind — they're now working through a strategy that does. Most people are used to riding an emotional roller coaster from statement to statement. The original advisor wasn't wrong to teach what he knows, but he never asked why the client accumulated that cash in the first place — in this case, the client had experienced "losing it pain" and didn't want to repeat that. This shows how insurance and market-based advising can complement each other with the right mindset, starting with what's genuinely best for the client rather than a one-size-fits-all rate-of-return pitch. The key question is always "why" — why have you accumulated this capital, why do you feel better in a cash position, what are you trying to accomplish next — rarely does rate of return come up in strategies clients actually love and want to implement; instead it's rate of control and peace of mind.

Another framing question: if you show up to retirement with $5 million in assets and no life insurance, versus $5 million in assets and $5 million in life insurance death benefit, which would you prefer? People always pick the one with the added death benefit. If the true cost of a policy could be shown to be returned many times over, why wouldn't you want that? Using Trent's words: the goal is to match a guaranteed event (death) with a guaranteed contract (life insurance) — when your death benefit equals or exceeds your estate, it gives you permission to enjoy your assets differently during life.

Closing: someone touting a great rate of return is simply playing by the rules they were taught, and there's nothing wrong with that — but the real question is what retirement actually means to you and what you're trying to accomplish. If you don't know, start having those conversations. Many people live day-to-day as if there will never be a "snowstorm," then don't know what to do when it hits, instead of proactively building a plan (the "Generac system") into their cash flow. As Nelson said, being in control of the banking process delivers the best benefits long range. Call to action: reach out to Nate, Brandon, or Brock, revisit Becoming Your Own Banker, and decide whether your current approach is creating the life you want or whether other options are worth exploring — and if you're comfortable being asked tough questions, they're the right guys; if not, call somebody else. Have a great evening.

episodes.title: You Are the Asset | Cashflow Legendz
episodes.text:
When you say "buy your net worth today," it's not a guess about the cost or whether you can afford it — you can show how money is already flowing through your life and where to prioritize paying for it today. You'll be glad to pay for it today because you'll know what to do with it as it works for you, instead of waiting 30 years at an unknown tax rate and unknown economic climate. Insurance companies operate off your gross income, not net income, since net is substantially less to work with. If your gross income is what you can lock in, you can make up for a lot of bad financial decisions made throughout your lifetime — essentially refunding those bad decisions back to your family.

Welcome to the Cash Flow Legends podcast with your hosts Nate, Brandon, and Brock. Remember, our insights are not direct financial advice, so consult with your financial team before making any decisions based on the topics discussed in this show.

Welcome back to Cash Flow Legends, Unlimited Life Concepts — Nate and Brandon this time. They're toying with the idea of eventually doing their own separate podcast alongside episodes with Brock, since Brandon and Nate sometimes have different conversations and Brock doesn't want to record live on Mondays — they're called to be good stewards of whatever opportunities they have.

Today's topic: their recent trip to the Nelson Nash Think Tank in Birmingham, Alabama — their fifth time attending in person (sixth if counting the virtual 2021 event). About 250 practitioners attended, plus guests from other teams in the Becoming Your Own Banker world. Resources are available at infinitebanking.org and the Nelson Nash Institute YouTube channel, where Nate and Brandon were once interviewed. Brandon got off the plane and immediately pulled up a "Conversations with Nelson Nash" playlist to listen to.

Most Mondays around 10am, Nate and Brandon do a faith-based book review — currently going through The 25 Biblical Laws of Partnership with God. Even running a household (not just a business) means operating in partnership with the Lord — businesses run on revenue and expenses, households on income and expenses, hopefully with a husband and wife who communicate well about it (they admit with humility they haven't always done this perfectly).

They had the privilege of speaking at the think tank, in the last slot after lunch on the final day. Nate's biggest takeaway was personal: love for the IBC community, and being recognized this year (a first) for people who consistently show up and add value — which led to conversations with newer members who might not have otherwise known to seek them out, given Nate and Brandon have been doing this eight years already. Brandon adds that people who've been doing it longer — offering encouragement, sharing their relationship and experiences with Nelson — made them feel accepted; a shoutout to community member Mary Jo. This is a small community whose goal is to build "the 10%," since if 10% of anything moves in the right direction it can have a tidal-wave effect that changes history — whole life insurance itself has existed for hundreds of years, but Nelson wrote Becoming Your Own Banker to bring the banking process down to the "you and me" level. Nearly everyone in the community, based on hundreds of conversations, is living and practicing Nelson's principles because of the impact on their finances, peace of mind, relationships, and businesses — and want to share it.

How they got started: it wasn't something they found, it found them, out of overflowing gratitude and excitement for what it did for themselves. April marks eight years since ULC started — a painful experience at times, but overall a blessing. Brandon brought his parents to the think tank this year; they attended his talk on stage. Their families live this mindset. Meeting mentors in person — James Neathery, Ryan Griggs, Mike Ever, Chris Bay, Mary Jo, Paul Fugere, Dave Befort, John Perrings, and more — reminded Brandon you can't put a price tag on longevity in relationships. Even brand-new attendees said there's "something different" about this community.

Nelson said: if you're not willing to read a 92-page book to potentially change your life and your thinking, they won't be able to help you. Worst case reading it, you learn something new — mentor Mike Ever has read the book over 600 times. The book itself started as a 10-hour, two-day seminar; attendees encouraged Nelson to write it down since it's easier to read a book than watch a 10-hour seminar on tape. Nelson realized he already had all the material — he just had to organize it.

This connects to today's topic: You Are The Asset. Brock wrote an article that morning about cost of capital, debt, and paying off debt, which ties back to being your greatest asset and how you think about how you think. A commenter, Rob, notes the 10 hours or reading the book kicks off a lifetime of learning. Nelson said: "This is all about how you think." They want to do life with people who love to think, learn, grow, and ask "what if" — because once you know the problem, the solution becomes simple, but then imagination takes over, which was the theme of their think tank talk. Nelson also said: when you understand the why, the how and the what make a lot more sense.

They walk through the human life value exercise from their talk. Most people believe they can buy as much life insurance as they want or can afford — not true. You can only buy as much as the insurance company is willing to offer, based on your human life value. Using their calculator: Brandon, 44, planning to retire at 65, with a $100,000 gross annual income, would be insurable for roughly $2.1 million — factoring in an average 4% annual income growth rate, that becomes about $3.2 million. So Brandon isn't a $100,000 asset, he's a $3.2 million asset. They role-play what it would be like if new-hire paperwork at any company listed your projected lifetime gross income and asked, "how much of that do you want to be sure goes to your family?" — framing life insurance not as a discussion about death, but about value. If your income stops, your mortgage, groceries, and childcare expenses don't — the bills continue but the engine stops.

Another role-play: Nate at 24, making about $40,000 gross as a coach (net was "rice and beans and pennies"), using a multiplier of 30 for lifetime value ($1.2 million), asking whether he'd want to protect that for maybe $10-20/month — since life insurance is never cheaper than it is today and you're never more insurable than today (20-year-olds can get millions in coverage for under $50/month). Nelson said life insurance should have been renamed a "personal monetary system" — a cash flow system with a death benefit. If whole life insurance were pitched as a bank product listing all its features (guaranteed income protection, guaranteed death benefit, ability to borrow against it while it grows uninterrupted, tax-deferred or tax-free growth), the line to sign up would be long — until you say the words "whole life insurance," and then people think of Dave Ramsey and back away. Nate and Brandon admit they used to think that way too, until they had a mindset revolution once they discovered the truth of what it really was.

A key point: just because something seems true doesn't mean it is — misclassification is dangerous. At the think tank, "slide over" quiz questions from Nelson's original 10-hour presentation often had obvious-seeming but incorrect answers. Example: the airplane "black box" is technically orange, not black, but everyone still calls it a black box.

Another feature highlighted: when borrowing against the policy's line of credit, you get to set your own terms for when and how it's repaid — unlike a bank loan. This won't make sense until you're willing to rethink your thinking, just like it didn't make sense to Nate and Brandon at first. Nelson's book, a workbook, opens with: "This is a workbook about the power of dividend-paying whole life insurance with a mutual company" — a workbook is something you return to often, and it hits differently at different seasons of life. For anyone unfamiliar with Nelson Nash, watching any clip on the Nelson Nash Institute YouTube channel reveals how logical, calm, and sound he was — no story about him does justice compared to hearing him talk directly. David Sterns (Nelson's son-in-law) has said he'd rather people know about Jesus than know about IBC, and that this isn't about the man, it's about the mission — about being able to lead your family better and take control of things that have been controlling you, connected to money.

If your income has grown over the past 10 years, does it make sense to have a static, fixed amount of death benefit protection, or should protection grow with your increasing human life value? Most people don't actively decide how much of their lifetime economic value should stay with their family — they just leave whatever's left, which isn't legacy, it's chance. If you ever find yourself saying "I hope" about any part of your financial strategy, that's not a strategy. Nate and Brandon don't claim to have it all figured out, but they know the rules of the game and can introduce them; you still decide how to play.

A key question: if life insurance had no cost at all, how much would you own? Most people answer "as much as possible" — because removing cost creates clarity around protection, certainty, responsibility, and legacy. What if you could recover the cost of your life insurance many times over throughout your lifetime by controlling the banking function, so it becomes your financial foundation rather than an expense? In hundreds if not thousands of conversations, when people see how their dollars can create an income plan letting them live life on purpose earlier, with less worry and doubt, they choose that every time — rate of return and the stock market become largely irrelevant by comparison.

Reframing the math: instead of chasing 10-20% rate of return on savings, what if you could make a guaranteed, tax-free/tax-deferred 2-4% on 30-70% of your income instead? Given that choice on paper, it's an easy pick. The more you control the banking function in your life, the greater opportunity to capture interest on dollars you'd otherwise never capture interest on. Money is going to flow through your life regardless — either you control how it flows, or someone else does.

Bringing it back to human life value: instead of spending 30-40 years building toward a certain net worth number, what if you could buy your net worth today and grow into it throughout your lifetime? This isn't guesswork — they show clients how money is already flowing through their life and where to prioritize paying for it today, so they don't have to wait 30 years at an unknown tax rate and economic climate; they can start living on purpose today. This unlocks people to dream and get creative again with their money, which can feel uncomfortable at first. Human life value is the future value of your present gross cash flow, not net cash flow — insurance companies operate off gross income.

On mortality: death has essentially a 100% track record (with one historical exception). If you're going to die for certain, and you already have money flowing through your life that could protect that guaranteed event with a product that reimburses your family while letting you control the banking function, why wouldn't you explore that? The barrier is usually that what you thought to be true isn't, and changing that requires laying down pride — something Brandon and Nate have had to do themselves repeatedly. Change in any part of life (money, relationships, fitness) usually requires a moment of admitting "maybe I didn't know what I thought I knew."

Closing: the think tank was a blessing, and they're honored to have spoken and to have seen so many people investing in their greatest asset — their ability to think. Whether wildly successful with money or struggling to keep money from flowing out of their lives, this mindset helps across the spectrum if you're willing to rethink your thinking. Call to action: reach out, get on Nate's schedule, send a message — there are countless ways to connect, and they'll help you become "the filter." Have a great one.

episodes.title: What Happens When Generations Think Together?
episodes.text:
Rate of return was number three in all the huge deals seen done — control and risk mitigation were always first and second, rate of return came after. If certainty or risk mitigation was wonky, scary, or unstable, the deal didn't make sense. Nelson thought on a 4-to-7-to-10-year long range because he thought like a forester — always asking "are we doing the best possible thing we can be doing for this person?" That means helping people get clarity on what's important to them and positioning their cash flow in alignment with their values.

Welcome to the Cash Flow Legends podcast with your hosts Nate, Brandon, and Brock. Remember, our insights are not direct financial advice, so consult with your financial team before making any decisions based on the topics discussed in this show.

Welcome back to Cash Flow Legends. Nate, Brock, and Brandon are excited — this episode is special because Nate and Brandon just got back from the Nelson Nash Think Tank, their fifth in person (sixth counting the COVID year). They never got to meet Nelson Nash in person — missed him barely — but have been blessed to connect with people who knew him well and were mentored by him for 10-25 years. Brock's dad, in a cool roundabout way, knew Nelson too. Brock takes over asking the questions, turning the tables the way Nate and Brandon usually grill him after conferences.

Nate's three biggest takeaways from this year's think tank: first, loving the IBC community and the Nelson Nash Institute — being in the room with people personally mentored by Nelson gives a greater sense of who he was and reignites the flame to perpetuate his legacy. Second, Nelson's wisdom is underrated until you dig deep into what he discovered — clips of Nelson in his later years shown throughout the week led Nate to the Nelson Nash Institute's YouTube playlist "Conversations with Nelson Nash" (about 35 videos, 2 to 30 minutes each) — even after reading Becoming Your Own Banker many times and teaching this for eight years, there's still so much wisdom in what he shares. Third, Nate and Brandon got to be keynote speakers this year, and from sharing what they've learned and the conversations afterward, they feel a greater confidence in the value they bring to the community than ever before.

Brandon piggybacks: their 45-minute talk spent the first 25 minutes on what they've learned over the last year or two and how people like Brock and his dad have impacted their thinking — Nelson talked a lot about how it's all about how one thinks, and the only way to challenge and grow in thinking is being around people willing to call you up on it. They polled the audience on experience level (0-25 policies sold = brand new) and more than half the room was brand new, which encouraged Brandon to keep doing what they're doing since many people are coming up behind them. It's humbling when someone says "I've been listening to your podcast" or "I know Brock" (from the podcast). The third takeaway: Nelson was emphatic that he wanted the message to go on not because of him, but because of the message and the truth — listening to that Nelson playlist reveals things that make you stop and realize gaps in your own thinking. One thing Brandon appreciated: this works at the "you and me" level, for anybody, if you're willing to rethink your thinking.

What they talked about to the group: the overarching theme was "You Are The Asset" — a two-layered conversation helping advisors understand how much of an asset they can be to the person in front of them, and also that they themselves are their greatest asset — the more conviction they have, the more confidence they can transfer to the prospect or client. They did a roleplay exercise on human life value, which several advisors in the room had never really thought through. Brandon notes that experienced advisors often know what human life value means but don't know how to frame questions to work backwards from it — a skill developed by being around people who ask uncomfortable questions that require sitting and thinking. Brandon did an off-the-cuff roleplay at dinner with a new firm member, Davis, walking through what a client visit would look like — that skill only comes from time and practice, and time and practice only happens when you decide you believe in something enough to live it. Brandon admires that Brock puts in work on learning and growing when nobody's watching, and wants his kids to think that way too — but also to ask whether the work is in alignment with being the hands and feet of Jesus, since misaligned effort can be more costly than slowing down to figure out where you're supposed to be bringing value.

They shared a visual framework: inside parentheses is DSB + TNT + SCA — "Do Simple, Better" and "Things that take No Talent" with "Small Consistent Actions" — representing what they can control. Outside the parentheses is "OG" — Only God, the beginning and end of time, above and around time, who knows it all; whenever Nate and Brandon think they're stepping outside those parentheses to do things their own way, they're reminded that doing simple better with small consistent actions that glorify the Lord is the best way to be. This visual pairs well with Nelson's five principles, particularly thinking long range and not being afraid to capitalize on what you can control. They encouraged the audience — mostly people wanting to teach what they teach — to put Nelson's framework over their business as a model: how are you thinking long range, working backwards from having "a place for windfalls," which was Nelson's sixth principle that didn't make it into the book because it's really succession/backward planning. Building a business that way means thinking beyond your own nose — about whether kids will be involved in the business, or if not, what that looks like (e.g., passing a book of business to Brock).

Nate quotes Nelson: "I'm a financial travel agent. If you don't know where you want to go, I can't help you get there. But if I can help you figure out where you want to go, I can definitely help you get there, maybe even more efficiently, with more peace of mind and certainty than you were already traveling." Brandon proposes calling their framework "founder SOPs."
