Brandon references James Clear (author of Atomic Habits): if you're in love with a dream but can't fall in love with the process to get there, you should give up the dream — you have to love the process as much as the destination.

On standout speakers: Brandon highlights Dr. Paul Cleveland, an economist who knew Nelson well for a long time. Asked by Ryan Griggs what made it hardest for him to understand the value of becoming your own banker through dividend-paying whole life insurance, Cleveland answered: "my college degree" — genuinely, not tongue-in-cheek, because he had to unlearn everything he'd been taught. Cleveland is likely in his 70s, a great reminder that the most dangerous thing anyone can suffer from is thinking they've "arrived" — Nelson's "arrival syndrome," which he spent the first half of his 92-page book addressing.

Nate highlights John, who brought data and charts destroying the mass-marketing message of "get as much cash value as early as possible and pay premiums for the shortest time possible." Even though Nate and Brandon already had that conviction, seeing it laid out that clearly built their confidence to a new level. It reinforced the importance of always asking "are we doing the best possible thing for this person" — and they know they are when helping people get clarity on what matters to them and aligning cash flow with their values.

Brandon adds on John: John was matter-of-fact but humble, not saying "you're wrong if you don't know this," just presenting the value of long-range thinking and reverse-engineering what happens if you cut off capitalization too soon. This paired with something Tim Ulrich said at a coaching academy: the first most important thing to understand is that you do not have to use whole life insurance to practice infinite banking — people try through checking accounts, farm equipment, leveraging land, etc. Nelson's book just showed that whole life insurance lets you do this more efficiently, with more certainty, control, and liquidity terms.

From one of Nelson's recorded conversations: his book examples showed capitalizing a policy over 4-5 years, ideally 10 years — but if an opportunity shows up in year five that's too good to pass up, having already positioned yourself with access to capital is a blessing ("you didn't steal the peas," so to speak).

Brock shares his prized possession: a first-edition copy of Becoming Your Own Banker that Nelson Nash personally gave to his dad in 2001, with notes throughout — a reminder of how important it is to have people who pioneered the space pour into you. It's been about 25 years since Nelson gave that copy to Brock's dad.

Another point from John: having spent most of his adult life around people spending large sums on tech investments, he confirmed that rate of return is number three in the biggest deals — control and risk mitigation come first and second. This ties to Nelson's long-range, multi-generational thinking — not just thinking about himself a year from now, but two, three, four generations down the road. Reaching greatness in anything requires consistent effort over time, not just talk — similar to how marriage isn't a perfect "soulmate" fantasy but requires sweat, tears, and struggle alongside the glorious and fun parts.

On AI: no keynotes specifically covered it, but a mastermind session shared AI tools used not for client-facing work but to help the advisors themselves be better versions of who they are. One tool Brandon is excited to use is an AI "brain dump" tool that helps reverse-engineer what you're really trying to get out of a jumble of thoughts and create a strategic approach — most of what's swirling in your head, once written down, won't happen the way you think, but getting it out of your head into a better place prevents mental "slush." Jason Lowe and Richard Canfield's training emphasized that everyone has unique capabilities that bring value to the marketplace, and the key is getting good at understanding and perfecting those capabilities.

Brandon closes: they learned from an experienced YouTuber they had lunch with that they haven't done a good job of humbly saying "we believe we can help you." There's no downside to reaching out, reading Becoming Your Own Banker, bringing questions, and seeing if it's a good fit. A key training takeaway: if you don't give something a date and specific time, you rarely get it done — dates and times register for accountability in the brain. If you feel like you can't find your financial rhythm or don't know where you want to go, reaching out costs nothing — worst case, you learn something new; best case, you form a relationship of lifetime generational impact. They hope everyone has a blessed day and look forward to the next episode.

episodes.title: Life insurance isn't just about death: cashflow legendz
episodes.text:
Today's chat: what does the middle class think about insurance compared to the wealthy, and how do millionaires or billionaires understand the importance and vitality of whole life insurance and insurance in general compared to Brandon or Nate when they were starting their working careers, and the 70-80% of other people similar to them. When someone's making a valuation on your company, part of that valuation is based on present cash flow. Human life value is similar — your human life value number is determined off your present cash flow; it's the future value of your present cash flow, in a sense. Garrett talks about the ability to essentially buy your net worth and then get to go play and build and grow into it simultaneously. That flips the conversation from "I need life insurance" to "wait, this is something I actually want in my life."

Welcome to the Cash Flow Legends podcast with your hosts Nate, Brandon, and Brock. Remember, our insights are not direct financial advice, so consult with your financial team before making any decisions based on the topics discussed in this show.

Welcome back to Cash Flow Legends. Nate, Brock, and Brandon catch up — Brock shares something from mentor Bob Castellon: a whole life insurance policy is a turbocharger to everything else in life. If you put all your money in the turbocharger and do nothing else, it won't do anything, because a turbocharger can't run the car on its own — it makes an engine run better. So if you have whole life insurance, you've got to use it for other assets already in your life.

Nate shares that he's been having more in-person conversations lately, joined a new BNI group, and keeps coming back to how many people misunderstand what life insurance really is — a conversation around human life value reframes everything, versus what people assume it is (just death benefit).

Brandon shares what he's been learning: if he gets emotionally upset arguing a point, he hasn't spent enough time understanding what he's discussing — the moment his emotional charge goes up, his logic and reasoning go down. He wishes he'd understood that in his 20s and 30s.

Getting into the topic: what does the middle class think about insurance compared to the wealthy, and how do millionaires or billionaires understand the importance of whole life insurance compared to Brandon and Nate when they started their careers, and the 70-80% of people similar to them. "Middle class" isn't a knock — it's the majority of income-earning people in America who foot the biggest bill, mostly out of a lack of awareness, not ignorance in an ugly way. One of the main things not understood: the myth that life insurance is just for dying, and you only need a little bit. If it were just for dying, wouldn't it be called death insurance? That's really what term insurance should be called — it's not life insurance, it's death insurance; nothing happens unless you die within the given time period. Permanent life insurance, whole life specifically, is guaranteed to be there when you pass away, but you also know you're guaranteed to die at some point — we all live until we don't. So permanent life insurance can be a living value; the death benefit can come alive and create other results for your family.

All the other insurance people carry — home, car, disability — is an "if this happens" product. Life insurance is a "when" product — the one thing guaranteed to kick in one day if it's in force is the death benefit. In their early working years, Brandon and Nate bought into the Dave Ramsey idea of "buy term, invest the difference," thinking they wouldn't need life insurance once debt-free. But Ramsey himself has said on his show he still has life insurance, because wealthy people understand that a permanent death benefit gives you permission to make different decisions in your life financially. Nate is going through the Retirement Income Certified Professional designation through the American College — retirement income planning is all about de-accumulation of assets, while wealth strategy is accumulation. There are decisions you get to make differently later in life if you have a death benefit equal to or greater than your estate.

Brock, who's been in rooms with more millionaires, shares that even very successful people — seven and eight figure exits — often say "I don't think I fully understand this" but have a desire to learn. Nelson called arrival syndrome one of the most dangerous things waiting to ambush you each morning. On the wealthier end, it's not uncommon for someone to say "I don't need life insurance, I've got plenty of money, but people keep telling me to look at it." Brock points out the absurdity: if you truly had "enough" money you wouldn't need anything, including writing checks to the government — nobody actually operates that way. It's the misuse of the word "need" — people don't need a 13,000 square foot home or a 4,000-bottle wine cellar they've never filled, but they want it. Life insurance is the same: not about need, it's about want — do you want to pay less in taxes, give more to family and charity rather than the government? He's seen low eight-figure clients who were told by nine- and ten-figure people "you need to go get life insurance" and don't understand why — there are levels to wealth, and some things some people can invest in that others can't. The wealthier someone is, the more comfortable they are having a year's worth of expenses saved; lower-income earners tend to feel "cash is trash" and want to deploy it elsewhere.

Nate ties this to business valuations and human life value again — everybody's human life value number and valuation is different, and the opportunity to secure that valuation is different, which shifts the conversation from "I need life insurance" to "I want this in my life," because it lets people take a deep breath about what they'll leave to kids and grandkids without worrying about disinheriting anyone while spending down assets in retirement, since there's a tax-free windfall going to the next generation.

Brock relates this to ULC's monthly "peace and perspectives" events, where members who a year ago thought life insurance was bad or unnecessary now can't wait to pay more premium and put policies to work creating new income streams — echoing Nelson's idea that imagination becomes one of the biggest things that occurs when people start rethinking their thinking. At a Nelson Nash coaching academy, someone who knew Nelson a long time pointed out that the concept of becoming your own banker is already happening in everyone's life somewhere — checking accounts, savings accounts, farm equipment, home equity, stock options — it's just not optimized. Nelson said becoming your own banker can include investments, but it's really about where you store your wealth first.

Nate recalls a Saturday conversation with Brock's dad, who practiced IBC for eight years after doing all the traditional things — maxed 401k, took the match, worked for a great company, retired. His dad's question: after working so hard to earn more, why would I want to make less money because the tax code scares me? He's 67-68 and still willing to rethink his thinking. This ties to a Todd Langford idea about "when every day is Saturday" — when things slow down, you spend more, like being on vacation every day, or you become a miser (Garrett's term) because you're afraid to spend.

What millionaires and clients headed that way begin to see: whole life becomes their "wealth warehouse" — a place to store capital and cash that helps improve everything else they're doing. At the end of the day it is life insurance, so their overall plan shows how they'll pass on their legacy not as a handout but a hand up — "let's keep this thing going for generations to come."

Clarifying a common concern: they are not eliminating traditional banks — banks are in the middle of all money flow. Instead of letting banks use your deposits solely for their benefit, you use the rules of the game to make deposits for your own family and future generations by paying premiums. Carlos Lara's book The Perfect Investment lists roughly 14 characteristics of an ideal investment — liquidity, control, tax advantages, etc. — and whole life insurance satisfies more of those characteristics simultaneously than people expect. If you stripped away the "whole life insurance" label and just described the product, people would think it sounds great — until you tell them the name, and their preconceptions kick in. Most people's understanding of whole life insurance is based on someone else's misunderstanding.

Brandon talks about getting more bold, with humility and grace, in inviting people to never stop rethinking what they think until they're confident they understand what something is or isn't — rather than letting people stop too early in their learning. It's a journey that can be uncomfortable, because you're taking old thinking out and putting new thinking in, then building new mental frameworks around it. The reward: people realize they can exert the same energy they've been exerting for years and gain — not by magic but by math — additional benefits just by changing where their dollars go. If there's still hesitation, it's almost always fear of doing something different than what everyone else is doing — including how to explain it to parents who've "hated whole life for 35 years." But Brock has also seen the flip side: parents and grandparents who come around once they realize they were sold a faulty product by an agent who wasn't teaching, coaching, or educating them, but just trying to "treat 'em and street 'em."

Final challenge for listeners, whether experienced with IBC or hearing this for the first time: book a call, get your questions answered, break the myths, bring your disagreements to the table and see what happens. If you're right that whole life insurance is bad, so be it — they'll come on and admit they were wrong about a hundred episodes' worth of content. If you believe whole life insurance is terrible, ask yourself why, and hop on a call to talk about it — there's no pressure to make decisions; the only decision on any call is whether you want to have another conversation. Closing thought, from Brock's dad Trent: "If what we thought to be true weren't, how soon would we want to know?" That applies to anything in life — faith, family, fitness, finances. They don't want to be the reason someone didn't get the opportunity to find out what they really know. You can go to cashflowlegendz.com and book a call with Nate for more resources.

episodes.title: Wealth Isn't Just Money | Cashflow Legends
episodes.text:
If we're going to get real simplistic, if I save money in a traditional checking account and I spend out of it, then I'm not really saving. I'm storing, but I'm not building up. So I think this is where getting clear on what saving, investing, and gambling is matters. Sixteen year olds have access to walking into casinos essentially — there is somebody in the market that is receiving their misguided ambition. In today's world when you look at finance, because of social media, which is the worst thing that's ever happened to finance, all you ever see are snapshots of the highlights of people's lives. You don't see all the in-betweens. And so when people see that and they hear about different stories, everybody's thought process around finances can pretty much be summed up as: they want the fastest route possible to massive amounts of money. They hear the stories of the lottery, the stories of investing in a moonshot and it changing their lives.

Welcome to the Cash Flow Legends podcast with your hosts Nate, Brandon, and Brock. Remember, our insights are not direct financial advice, so consult with your financial team before making any decisions based on the topics discussed in this show.

Welcome back to Cash Flow Legends. You see two guys that are missing somebody — Nate is out of town today watching some state championship basketball for his kids' school. Brock and Brandon catch up on golf, families, and the school baseball season before getting into the topic.

So, Brock, we're going to talk today about your crowd and anybody coming into your age, but it's relevant for me in my 40s too, so we can speak from both ends of the spectrum — what you've experienced, what you see daily, what I've experienced and see looking back starting in my early 20s thinking about what money was. It kind of started from a podcast you were listening to, but it keeps coming up in conversations about how we view money, investing, gambling, and saving.

We were at a conference not too long ago where Michael Phelps was talking, and I've been helping another advisor build out a "get your finances in order" program. We kept coming back to the fact that in today's world, because of social media, all you ever see are snapshots of the highlights of people's lives — you don't see all the in-betweens. Everybody's thought process around finances gets summed up as wanting the fastest route to massive amounts of money — that's the goal for most people in America. It's not a bad goal, but is it reality? Probably not. They hear the stories of the lottery, of a moonshot investment changing their life. But the reality, and this ties back to Michael Phelps — somebody asked him what made him so great, what made him different. He said it wasn't that he was so much better than everyone else; he won his races by a hundredth of a second. What created the greatness for him, how he defined greatness, was the daily stacking of habits every single day. He just did the same thing over and over again. That's what we've got to bring it back to when it comes to wealth building: wealth takes time. That's why we have the concept called the time value of money — it takes time to increase the value of money you have. Without consistency, without time, without growth, money doesn't go anywhere.

That reminds me of something Nelson Nash talks about — the idea of thinking long range and not being afraid to capitalize. Let's say Brock graduates high school and comes into the market, green, ready to go, thinking "how can I take money to make money?" The first thing to coach yourself up on is getting real clear on what wealth is at your current age, your experiences, where you live, what you're doing. Write down on one piece of paper what wealth means to you — it would be way different than what it means today, but at least you'd have a start.

The second piece Nelson talked about all the time: words matter, and proper classification of words. Investing and saving, investing and gambling — these are misrepresented in the market and on social media all the time. This came from a podcast with Morgan Housel and Chris Williamson, where they talked about how when young men start out, investing is gambling to them because it's based on sports gambling logic — "I know how to bet on this stock and sell it high." Buy low, sell high — that's the game they're taught. Therapist offices are full of young men right now who've lost all their money sports gambling or "investing" recklessly. That was Brock at 18 — he put $500 into E-Trade thinking he'd get rich on a moonshot, didn't understand any of it, kept losing money, gave up, came back years later and found it was worth 30 bucks. He's since learned he wasn't the only one — Morgan Housel showed the data on how many young men struggle with this, and even 10th graders talk about losing $20,000 trading, not realizing they're gambling, not investing.

Breaking the three words down: saving is the act of putting money in a place that cannot lose. Investing is going through the fundamentals, the technical analysis, doing proper due diligence to learn whether something is a good deal or bad deal. Gambling is saying "that looks good today, I'll take it and hope for the best." Most people live in the gambling space. There are also two types of saving: saving in the traditional sense — checking account, savings account, qualified plan — and saving money by paying premiums into a whole life policy. Those are different because saving means locking in and knowing you won't lose dollars; if you save in a traditional checking account and spend out of it, you're not really saving, you're storing but not building up.

Sixteen-year-olds now have access to walking into casinos essentially through the internet — someone in the market is receiving their misguided ambition; the money didn't disappear, it transferred from their account to somebody else's. The solution as parents is teaching a system you can course-correct with more quickly, one aligned with what wealth actually means, rather than expecting to hit a home run every time. It's not money itself people want — it's the outcome the money could provide. Most people in retirement planning spend too much time figuring out what to do with the money and too little time figuring out what they're going to do in retirement. Morgan Housel's book The Art of Spending offers one equation: independence plus purpose. Most people want independence, but independence without purpose leads to problems — getting sick, retreating, depression. Many in the FIRE (financial independence, retire early) movement retired at 28, did it for a couple years, and fell into massive depression because they had no purpose, and went back to work.

If we're created in the image of God, to be his hands and feet, to love him and love others, then it's silly to think we wouldn't have purpose on this earth, and retiring just to stop working toward a purpose is like "oceanfront property in Arizona" — an illusion. A recent conversation with a family member illustrated this: asked what he brings in a month after all his time and energy, then asked if he'd be doing the job the same way if that money came in automatically — he said no, he keeps the job for flexibility, schedule, and benefits. Asked how far out he sees himself working, he said maybe to 60 doing the same thing — but he wasn't sure he'd have that income at 60 if nothing changed. When asked if retiring at 50 instead, by changing how money is allotted and flows, would be worth exploring, he said absolutely. People stay with what they've been doing because they don't get around people who ask them questions that make them think differently.

Reframing at 18: top three things to tell your younger self, no matter what — invest in yourself first, structure your cash flow the right way, learn how to be generous. You can never overinvest in yourself as long as you know whose you are, because that gets you around the right people and mindsets and conversations. From that, generous awareness becomes clearer — being generous is a gift from the Lord, not a responsibility you don't want. Then build a financial plan that doesn't require "the snakes and the dragons" — banks and Wall Street — because it's not necessary to live a life full of peace if you control your time, schedule, energy, and effort. That would mean no gambling in the market, paying as many whole life premiums as possible on as many people as you have insurable interest in, and understanding that rate of control — how much money you're controlling that's flowing through your life — matters more than rate of return on a screen.

It's not the money people want — it's the thing they think the money needs to do for them, and if they lose clarity on that and stop doing the thing that defines them, they lose their purpose because it became an idol. Nobody's immune to poor money decisions — even the founder of behavioral finance said when asked what he took away from all his research, "nothing," because he's human too. Even someone raised by a father who knows finance can make the same mistakes at 18 with a first paycheck — spending it on watch subscriptions, golf box subscriptions, clothes, just because the money is coming in and it feels good. Being a good steward isn't throwing money at the wall just because you can. Just because you have money to invest in something doesn't mean you should — that's basically how this whole conversation started. Nelson always said "opportunity finds capital," and there are different types of capital based on who controls the rules.

Getting sued taught the importance of having a plan not for if things don't go according to plan, but for when things don't go according to plan — there are two lawsuits every minute in America. An advisor to some of the wealthiest families in America said if there's one thing he'd tell anybody, it's to have more liquidity than you think you need, because no plan goes entirely to plan — something's going to go wrong. Just because you have the money doesn't mean you need to invest it. Not every deal is a good deal — every bad deal starts with a great story, and if you think you've found the greatest investment ever, there will always be another one right behind it. If a decision is causing you to lose sleep or peace of mind, move on.

A fourth principle: have a framework for any amount of money you're going to spend beyond daily expenses. Ask — is it pleasing to the Lord? Is the person we're doing business with shady or lacking integrity? What's the best case that could happen (the mind loves to lean into the positive because it's exciting)? What's the worst case that could happen? And are we okay with the worst case? That's from The Road Less Stupid: what's the good outcome, what's the bad outcome, can I live with the bad outcome?

Foundational principles: spend less than you make — that's number one. Hopefully save 15% of your income, store up provisions so that when something comes along you can handle it. Once you've stored up provisions and taken care of yourself, it's time to take care of others. From the Wealth Without Wall Street guys: before spending money, ask does this increase my income or reduce an expense — those should be the only two questions. It sounds simple, almost silly not to have thought of it that way before, but simplicity is the point — you could give the same framework to your kids and get clarity from them just as easily as from yourself.

The book Effortless discusses how tough problems that seem like a "money problem" might actually be a "principle problem" instead of a "method problem." Methods are internet ideas, quick hitters that sound great and feel good fast. A principle is foundational — it takes longer than you think, costs more, and has more unexpected things happen than not; when it occasionally goes exceptionally well and you make a lot of money fast, that's not the norm. Principles work everywhere — relationships, business partnerships, parenting, dating conversations with your teenager — because they're foundational, which is why they're called principles.

If starting over, the core principles would be: figure out what life you want and write it down, understanding it will change over time (you might even be a little ashamed looking back at what you wrote ten years ago). Give away the first 10%, whether religious or not. Spend less than you make, save 15%. Store up three to six months of expenses. Protect against all catastrophic risk. Then go invest your money, getting clear on what you invest in and why — the best investments are in and through your business, your family, and yourself. And get real clear on where wealth is stored — the environment — because storing wealth in a whole life policy gives more advantage and runway to create as you go.

If you're just starting out and trying to build clarity: figure out what kind of life you want to live, knowing it will change, and start building sound principles around that. Looking back, it's uncertain whether either of them would have listened even if someone had told them all this at 18 — but that's why it helps to be around people who are experts in different fields, since the more you understand something, the more you realize how much you don't understand.

Call to action: if you heard any of this and thought "I wish I could take some action on that" — take action. What's the worst thing that's going to happen? You'll find out something new that is or isn't for you. Reach out, read Becoming Your Own Banker, get on the schedule, do something different than what you've been doing. We'd love to visit with you and see if we can bring value — and if we can't, at least we got to meet each other. Have a blessed day.

Most people believe they can buy as much life insurance as they can afford. That is not true. You can only buy as much life insurance as the insurance company is willing to offer you. It's important for whoever advisor you're working with to be extremely interested in what brings you the most peace of mind in your life.

Yeah, and Nate, it's very common, as we were talking about on the podcast this morning — I'm going to pull up a graphic that you created that we use a lot. It's very common for people to be on the normal, left side of this ride option early on and think that's just normal, and not be aware of the fact that they may not always want the feeling of that downward gravity pull and that upward swing and that stomach-turning feeling as they age. And the way on the right is kind of how we view money. It's the same energy just producing a more efficient result.

It's interesting, Nate. All my middle school principal years, we would go to Six Flags as our big trip at the end of the year. When that began, I was around 30, and man, I would ride every one of those rides — besides the spinning ones. Absolutely loved it, didn't notice anything negative about it. Each year that I got through my principal years, especially the last few when I was 37, 38, 39, I started noticing there was a pull or drag on me on those roller coaster rides that I did not like — that I had to choose which one I really wanted to ride and stayed off the other ones. Yeah. And also something that's left out of a lot of these conversations around having traditional retirement accounts is not only do you ride this roller coaster of emotions from the highs and lows, but you also don't fully know what is yours when it comes to that statement, because we're creating on a pre-tax strategy. We are effectively creating an unknown debt to the government to be determined by them at a later date, because we're going to be taxed at income, not investment rates, and we don't know what the taxes are going to be in the future. That's why we are strong proponents of post-tax type strategies, whatever that looks like for you — simply because you're getting the uncertainties of life out of the way in those later years when you need more certainty in your life. When I look at my whole life policy statement, one, I never get a statement from the insurance company that says we had a down year and here's the result, you have less money than you did the year before you put in. Two, I know that death benefit number is a guaranteed number that gets kept in my family. I know that the cash value, which is the equity — that's the portion of the death benefit that's recognized as money we can use in our life right now. I know that by contract that money is money I have access to, to put to work in different areas of my life.

Yeah, Nate, that brings a very vital piece to why we love teaching this. And if you come to pizza and perspective, you're going to hear this throughout: we are not telling you that you have to pick whole life insurance over your retirement plan, or over a great rate of return in an investment. What we are saying is what Nelson said in Becoming Your Own Banker — the process of banking goes on forever, which certainly can include investments. But Nate, I want to zoom out. 70 to 80% of the people that we worked with at first, which is where we were when we started — all that tax conversation that you just had that makes sense to me and you and a lot of our clients that have been doing it for a while, it flew right over my head some way or another eight to ten years ago. So at a simple level, if somebody would have said to me and you, Nate, "Hey, you can work the same amount of effort you already are applying and get a better, more efficient peace of mind result" — or set another way, you can keep more of what you earn so that you can continue to get better at learning how to earn more with what you keep — that really sums it up. And it doesn't create this competition that the general marketing scheme by the big three — banks, Wall Street, and the IRS — have created.

And I think, Nate, why we love the pizza and perspectives and the in-person events is because we get to hear our clients' or members' stories, and we also get to see others who are beginning their journey of rethinking their thinking, and they get to ask questions like, "What practically made sense to you finally that allowed you to start adding this into your approach?" In this picture, we're looking at a roller coaster on one side, which we call normal — the roller coaster goes up and down — and then we've got IBC on the other side, and it's a rocket ship with an upward trajectory. The reality is we have people who are still in both camps in their life. They still have the normal 401k that they're operating with, but they also have IBC that they're implementing simultaneously. And when you are working in both camps, those roller coaster moments don't seem so hectic anymore because you've got that certainty that you started building in for yourself.

One of the things that Brock talked about, and we talk about often, is this idea of "permission to spend," which is a book written by Tom Wall where he lays out very eloquently and very powerfully what a whole life policy can do in the life of a retiree as a volatility buffer. So we'll touch on that real quick. I think this will help anybody — the number of conversations, Nate, that you and I have with people who go, "I've been watching what you've been talking about, but I've been too worried to really reach out because I feel like I'm committing to something I don't understand." We want to flip that on its head. We want to say we want to be sure that you are confident in why whole life insurance can help what you're already doing be more effective, create more peace of mind, create more certainty.

So that volatility buffer, Nate, at a high level — Nate and I could do all of our retirement planning in the traditional sense of qualified plans. We say 401k because that's what most people know, but it could be a 403b, teacher retirement system, all kinds of different qualified plans. And Nate could retire a year before me. If he's pulling all of his income percentage-wise off of the accumulated assets that are coming through the market, he could live a great life where his assets only go up, or go up enough that he can retire in a way where he never experiences anything chaotic. I could retire a year later and experience a down year and pull off of that in that down year and never recover, and be out of money in a couple of years. That is what we're talking about with the roller coaster.

So I think something we didn't do well early on, Nate — not because we weren't trying, it's just we didn't know what we didn't know — is articulating, explaining, discussing how this approach to life, no matter where you are in your financial steps — whether you have no savings, whether you don't know how to keep your money, whether you've got a large accumulation of savings in different accounts, whether you're somewhere in between — Nelson's message in Becoming Your Own Banker and sound money thinking can positively impact any household if they're willing to apply it.

And Nate, I want you to talk to this reality of even if you're not saving any money, even if you don't have a retirement plan, even if you're like, "there's no way I can afford to pay for premiums for a whole life policy" — how would you go back and coach yourself up, knowing what you know now, to counter that thought process? Well, the thing that we always want to make sure is that our cash flow is in alignment with our values and the things that we love and want to be a part of. And I think that's an important question a lot of people don't really ask often: are the places that I'm sending money to right now really in alignment with who I am? You and I both had this conversation early on and continue to have it — we feel like our money is more in alignment with who we are today than ever before. So alignment of cash flow is going to be really important whether you start a whole life policy or not. One of the things that's also really important is understanding your lifetime economic value is a real number whether you plan for it or not.

So Nate, in Becoming Your Own Banker — because we're doing a Becoming Your Own Banker walkthrough where we go through every section on our podcast, Cash Flow Legends, and we just recorded one this morning (we're ahead a couple weeks, or behind, however you want to think about it — it's not going live as soon as we record it, this will be a couple weeks) — I was reminded again of how important it is to read Becoming Your Own Banker if you're at all interested in this. It starts with this important piece that this is about the power of dividend-paying whole life insurance and how one finances the things of life. The first page also says it can include investments and the things of life, but it is about how one finances the things of life. And Nate, if I could go back and coach me and you up, this is what I would say to anybody listening that's new to this: what is the downside of exploring this? I would get real clear on the answer to that eight years ago when we were just starting, because what I could now tell you is I learned something new — even if I never changed my behavior, or where my dollars flowed. But what you and I have learned over and over again is when you're willing to, as Nelson said, rethink your thinking, this creativity, this imagination, this excitement starts taking over because people begin to realize things — they begin to see inefficiencies in their life, they start to understand what the problem really is. And it's that someone is always controlling the banking function in your life — it's going to be you or it's going to be somebody else. The process of banking is going to go on no matter what. No matter what happens in life, there's always going to be a banking process, and someone is always going to be benefiting from that process.

Welcome to being partners. So when you were talking about learning, leaning in, exploring — what's the worst case scenario? The funny thing is, I know when you and I first heard about Dave Ramsey and the things he was talking about, we didn't have to go through this big process of thinking, "Hey, what's the worst case scenario for me to learn more about this?" It was almost more of an instinct of like, "All right, he's talking about something that may have some value, I need to find out more about that." So you don't have to make this massive commitment to yourself to start leaning in and learning about this stuff. It's really an easy decision: do I want to know more about what they're talking about, or do I want to choose to ignore that? There's not a huge decision-making process that has to take place just to learn.

All right, Nate, so let's touch on that for just a second. Nelson says in Becoming Your Own Banker, first of all, that this is a workbook. So you can go to our website — you don't want to ever talk to us until you've got all your questions together. This is the best piece of advice I can give anybody: go get Becoming Your Own Banker, get it in your house, and ask your spouse to go on a journey with you of learning something new, because you're not going to be able to explain it — you're still learning, they're not going to have any context. Have a piece of paper beside you and write down the questions that come up as you're reading it fairly quickly — don't get bogged down into the details, just read it fairly quickly — and then spend time discussing with your spouse or loved one or family what your current knowledge is, to be able to answer that question.

So what does it mean to control the banking process? That sounds real scary. It sounds real scary for me, Nate — I was like, what the heck does that mean, I don't understand that. But if somebody would say to me, then it just means money's flowing in and out of your life. Somebody's going to benefit from it, somebody's going to control it, somebody's going to set the rules — you can, or somebody else can. When I hear the word cash flow now, Nate, I know that means extra money on top of living life that I can save. But what I also know, Nate, is that cash flow can be created with your current income production ability just by having somebody else ask you different questions about how money's flowing through your life. So we're not saying you've got to go make more money — we're actually saying often, Nate, that if you learn this, what infinite banking really does with where you put your money first, it will increase your ability to get more benefit out of the dollars you're already earning. And those things are where we really spend a lot of time in person discussing. And the only thing it's going to cost you — let's think about real cost, Nate — is 20 bucks or 25 bucks to buy the book. That's the only thing it's going to cost you. Everything else is going to be your time and energy. And what I love about this is it's going to bring you to the forefront of, where's my energy going currently? Because the roller coaster is all good till it isn't.

The roller coaster — I might want to stay on it my whole life. I might be that 89-year-old that just loves riding a roller coaster forever, but what if I want to get off? Can I? Brock brought up a great point this morning, Nate. He said, what if you want to volunteer at church for a position that's paid, and you want to volunteer, and you know your income continues to come in off of your assets and what you know about money in a way that you can tell the church, "I don't want to be paid, I want you to redirect that money somewhere else, I am excited about doing this. I control my time, my energy, my effort, and where I put it, and this is what I'm committed to for the next year." That's really what understanding money gets us to. That's really what we spend a lot of time getting to do and try to get better at, Nate, because we're still learning every day how we can ask better questions to show up for us or our members and go, "What does it look like when you get off the roller coaster ride?" And Nate, the cool thing is, when you ask those questions, people's eyes start lighting up, or there's an awkward pause. They light up because they go, "I'm thinking about money propelling what matters to me most." Or they pause because they go, "I've never thought about that before." And then you get to go, why haven't you?

Why don't people normally think about that? What's a reason or two that you hear often where they go, "I've never been asked that question"? Because everybody's conditioned to believe that they're going to work till they're 65 or 70, for this magical age where one day they can start to slow down. And kind of what you were talking about earlier — when you start to create more efficient cash flow, you don't have to slow down, but you do take some pressure off yourself from having to get out there and bust it every day, so to speak. Most people just assume that their working years are up to 65 or 70 because that's what they see everybody else doing and that's what they've been told. And also, they've been given rules around their money as far as when they can access it. One of the things that Brock said that you'll hear on another podcast if you listen to it later is: we assume that we're going to make it to a certain age and we're going to have all of our choices, all of our faculties intact. But he was talking to a 68-year-old who is a go-getter, who is very successful, who you would never know is 68, and he said, "I've got 15, 18 buddies that did not get to choose what retirement looked like for them because of some version of a medical event that they did not know was going to occur, like dementia or some other thing that took away those years that they've been working so hard to get to."

So it's not ever fun to think about those things, Nate, but we were equating it to the snowstorm we've been having, with the ice and the freezing in our area. Nobody ever says, "I'm going to go buy a generator in the middle of the summer because there's a snowstorm coming." But everybody that has the generator and knows the plan for when the snowstorm comes in and when electricity is lost always seems to be living with more contentment and peace of mind than those who are frantically — I'm one of them — running to the store to get a generator and there aren't any. And if I were to say what we spend the most time doing with our members across almost all states and all conversations and ages, it's getting real clear on helping them understand what peace of mind means today, tomorrow, one year, three years, five years from now — and most importantly, the flexibility to adjust when life changes, because it's going to change, isn't it, Nate? There's no straight line for sure.

Well, and you think about the thought process that goes into purchasing a generator to begin with. People don't buy generators because it's going to put cash in their pocket. They buy it for convenience and for comfort. They buy it in the event when things don't work out the way they thought they were going to work out. And so if we're talking about this roller coaster — if you're in the market, you're going to have down years. It's pretty much a guarantee that you're going to have down years if you're in the market. So if you know that, especially in retirement years, when you're faced with this risk of sequence of returns and trying to make sure that you're not — well, you've got a generator that kicks in, so to speak, one of those auto switches on it — that kicks in on those down years so that you're not sitting in the dark. That's exactly right — you're not freezing your tail off because the heat's not running, and you have a place for your loved ones to come because you can take care of them because you have planned.

And this is really, Nate, if I could sum it up in one sentence to really simplify it all: the energy and effort you're already using — if it could be redirected to create a better result, why wouldn't you explore it? And "better results" is different for everybody. Nate, ours has evolved eight years in, because we've gained more peace of mind, we've gained more certainty and control. Have we figured it all out? No. Do we still feel like there's a long ways to go? Yes. That is man's nature — for there to be friction in creating value in this world. It's scriptural — we're going to toil in the earth, we're going to labor. So that's going to be there. But as we go through that, probably one of my favorite things that we get to do, Nate, when we meet with people in person at pizza and perspective, is encourage people to keep leaning into what peace of mind really means for them.

Yeah. And I know at 44, peace of mind to me is not the Texas Giant anymore. It was definitely at 24, and at 14, and maybe at 34 — but at 44, I think I'll be okay if I never ride the Texas Giant again. I might get a wild hair, you know, if I end up there before too long. But you get the point — we don't have to be on the roller coaster ride, and if we want to get off of it, we want to be able to stop the ride and get off of it whenever we want to — fully stopped, not jumping while the thing's still moving, trying to figure out how we're going to survive.

So, pizza and perspective this Saturday, the workshop — we've got 12, 13 spots remaining. We only have about 20 to 25 because we want it to be personal. If we have somebody new there that hasn't been in or around our community before, we want them to be sure they're comfortable. We'll feed you Pro's pizza around 11:30. That doesn't cost you anything other than your commitment and willingness to show up and be open-minded. That's it. If you want to wait to ask your questions there, great. You can always send us questions here. You can go get Becoming Your Own Banker — that's the foundation of everything we teach. But we confidently know, Nate, that we can bring value to anybody who's wanting to bring more value to themselves than anything else. And that's what we look forward to. So hope to see you this Saturday and hope you have a great day. If you watch this later, hope it brings value to you if you watched it now. Thank you for being here. See you.

episodes.title: Zig Ziglars Secret to Wealth: Prisoner of Hope
episodes.text:
Zig Ziglar says that surely one of the saddest experiences in life is to hear someone say, "If I could only talk, run, jump, sing, dance, think, or concentrate like him or her," and the voice trails off in silence. The message is: if I just had someone else's ability, what wouldn't I do? Here's the gut punch, the answer is that you would not do a thing with someone else's ability if you are not using the ability you already have. Comparison is where we believe that somebody has something that, if we had it, we would be able to do what they're doing — and Ziglar says that's simply not true. Reality is we're always telling ourselves some kind of story, and if you apply logic to it, it never makes sense to tell a story of scarcity or negativity when nothing has actually occurred. Yet that's what we deal with so much in our lives, because we're naturally drawn to negativity. That's why the news is always negative — it sells.

Welcome to the Cashflow Legendz podcast with hosts Nate, Brandon, and Brock. These insights are not direct financial advice, so listeners should consult their own financial team before making decisions based on the topics discussed.

Nate and Brandon open by explaining the purpose of the show: they talk about so many things with people who encourage them to grow and invest in themselves that they decided to start recording those conversations and sharing the value. Today's topic comes from Zig Ziglar's book See You at the Top, specifically a section called "Prisoners of Hope." Ziglar has since passed away, but his ideas remain influential.

Some people are prisoners of fear, and others are prisoners of habit — both are Ziglar statements. But what if instead we were prisoners of hope? What if the only thing keeping us stuck is what we believe about our future? Nate connects this to an idea from Myron Golden about the stories we make up in our heads about things that haven't even happened — comparing it to sitting in the driveway burning gas without ever driving anywhere. Most of the time we're stuck because we've created a story in our minds that isn't even true. Whether we respond to something with a positive or negative story in our minds, if nothing has actually occurred yet, both are just stories we've told ourselves. The reality is we're always telling ourselves some kind of story, so it rarely makes logical sense to choose one of scarcity or negativity.

Brandon reads directly from Ziglar's book: when we are prisoners of circumstance or habit, we're really letting our circumstances dictate the habits that keep us imprisoned in how we think and live, which is often connected to comparison. Prisoners of hope, by contrast, are captured by something forward-looking — by hope itself. Being captured by hope means being a long-term thinker, not focused on the past or held down by things that have already occurred, but looking ahead. Nate draws a parallel to the wise men in the Christmas story, who spent hundreds of years looking ahead in anticipation of the Messiah.

Brandon shares that a prisoner of hope is someone who refuses to let current circumstances have the final word — and admits he's often guilty of letting one circumstance dictate his thinking for the next day, week, month, or year. A prisoner of hope stands in direct contrast to a prisoner of circumstance. A prisoner of circumstance says things like "this is just how life is," blames the economy, upbringing, or timing, and lives reactively and short-term. Referencing Myron Golden, Brandon notes that just as there can't be a front of a piece of paper without a back, there can't be hope without its opposite. A prisoner of hope is future-focused, thinks long range, acts before results show up, and lives from conviction rather than conditions.

Nate reflects that this connects to being reactionary versus proactive, and that being proactive requires being settled in one's convictions. He and Brandon then discuss why they started recording these conversations: after a founders' retreat at a lake, they committed to starting their week together intentionally, with scheduled accountability time. Nate and Brandon are business partners, and Brandon jokes that describing Nate as his "partner" in public makes him uncomfortable until he clarifies "business partner" — though there are real similarities between business partnership and marriage in terms of closeness and shared conviction. They mention a new book they're reading together, The 25 Biblical Laws of Partnership with God.

Discussing accountability, Nate explains that by God's grace they've become self-aware enough to recognize when they're slipping into unhelpful thinking, and have given each other permission to call it out. Each of them offers the other a different perspective when needed. Brandon says he has no doubt 2026 will be meaningful because of this new weekly rhythm, even though it's new and imperfect. He reflects that as business owners — and more importantly as sons of God and brothers of Jesus — they've learned they'll never fully arrive; there's always something new to learn. This is part of why they started the show: people frequently come to them with financial questions, and while they're not the ultimate answer, they know who is, and they simply have knowledge about money that brings more peace, clarity, and purposeful living.

Brandon highlights that hope is not passive. There's a passive form of hope, like hoping to win the lottery, but real hope tied to conviction creates behavior. Hope is not wishful thinking — it produces preparation, discipline, delayed gratification, and faithful action before clarity arrives. Hope is fuel that keeps people moving when motivation fades. Because the heart can be deceitful, as scripture says, hope needs to be tied to foundational truths. Nate agrees, adding that ideas need real-life, personal application — it's not enough to just read and learn; you have to apply things in a way that fits your own life rather than mimicking someone else's path.

Brandon brings up a text exchange from the night before, when both were in a bit of a funk. He jokingly referenced the definition of insanity — doing the same thing over and over expecting a different result — and asks whether people are prisoners of hopeful thinking that helps them grow, or prisoners of hopeless thinking. If you're a hopeless thinker who questions the benefit of hopeful thinking, Ziglar's challenge is to ask: compared to what? Has hopeless thinking actually produced good results and relationships, or has it kept you down? Brandon poses a broader question: if nothing externally changed for the next twelve months, would your internal posture stay the same? Nate connects this to the idea that complacency can be internal, and that there's a fine line between healthy contentment and complacency that they have to be careful not to cross.

Brandon adds that for driven providers, there's always tension between providing for loved ones and remaining content, and says with certainty that navigating that tension starts and stops with one's relationship with Jesus Christ — a lesson learned by trying it other ways and finding they don't work as well long-term.

They move to practical steps for becoming a prisoner of hope. One is to use future-oriented language: stop saying "if" and start saying "when." Nate shares that the practice that's brought him the most value is that whenever he's faced with a circumstance that would ordinarily send him to a negative place, instead of saying "I have to do XYZ," he says "I have the privilege of doing XYZ." Privilege forces him to define why something is a privilege, which pushes him into gratitude — and, referencing something Tim Tebow said recently, you can't be in comparison and gratitude at the same time. When you're in gratitude, darkness runs.

Another practical tool is journaling, which lets you reflect on things to be grateful for, celebrate wins, and revisit prayers that were answered in unexpected ways — things people often forget they even prayed for unless they wrote them down.

A final action step: do today what tomorrow's version of you will thank you for. To know what that looks like, you have to get clear on what you want tomorrow's version of yourself to be. Nate and Brandon use a "four Fs" framework — faith, family, fitness, and finance — which don't operate in separate compartments but work together, sometimes with more tension than balance, echoing Tim Tebow's preference for the word "tension" over "balance." Time under tension is where growth occurs, whether in fitness, in an oak tree's root system growing stronger under strain, or in a baby giraffe that's dropped to the ground at birth and kicked by its mother until it stands — tension and discomfort that ultimately serve its survival.

Turning to the new year, Nate suggests a practical framework for anyone without written goals: write down "a year ago I was ___, and now I am ___," aiming to look back in twelve months and see real progress. Brandon connects this to a principle from Dan Sullivan: first declare where you want to go, even if it's fuzzy, then pick measurable checkpoints between now and then, and reflect on progress without self-criticism if it falls short. He shares his own experience giving up alcohol as an example of how one small change compounds over months. He also notes that the brain, while less than 2% of body weight, consumes about 20% of daily caloric intake. Nate shares that a health coach pointed out he was running mostly on adrenaline rather than proper nutrition, and that he — like Brandon — tends to operate on momentum and hype. Both take action quickly once convinced of something, but sustainability and follow-through are where they need outside accountability.

Closing out, Brandon reflects that they can't control everything about their current circumstances, but they are in control of believing in where they're going. They wrap up thanking listeners for their time, noting that after eight years running their company, Unlimited Life Concepts, and sharing on the Cashflow Legendz podcast, it's ultimately not about the money but about purpose, clarity, and moving toward something greater than themselves.

episodes.text:
Most people were taught to follow the rules with money: save it, spend it, borrow it, pay interest, and hope retirement works out. But what if the rules were written by the very system keeping you stuck? Welcome to Cashflow Legendz, the show where Nate, Brandon, and Brock challenge conventional financial thinking, expose the hidden leaks in your cash flow, and help families and business owners build more control, certainty, and legacy. This show is for educational purposes only, not financial, tax, or legal advice.

The hosts open by sharing what they're each grateful for that week — Brandon talks about conviction from a Sunday sermon about not making excuses for small compromises, Brock is thankful for warmer weather, and Nate is thankful for a business partner who holds him accountable and for time spent watching his son at soccer practice.

They then turn to a section in Nelson Nash's Becoming Your Own Banker that asks, "What if I am uninsurable?" The deeper question, they argue, is whether people are even asking the right question in the first place. Nelson wrote the book for the layperson, not for insurance professionals, and he didn't want anyone to reach the end of the book and conclude the concept wasn't for them just because they couldn't personally qualify for a policy. Being uninsurable doesn't disqualify someone from applying these principles in their life.

Brock notes that people need to accept that being uninsurable is a real possibility — he's currently working with a breadwinner client who wanted to put a policy on his wife instead because her health ratings were better, which is ill-advised. Brock would rather a client have a less efficient policy than none at all. Nate explains underwriting in simple terms: insurance companies use actuarial charts based on height, weight, and health to assign a rating (preferred, standard, etc.), and there are no "deals" in insurance — just the average cost. Getting qualified and understanding the need for banking matters more than the specific rating you land.

Nate shares an example of a client whose health had improved after previously being declined, so he came back to get qualified — like getting pre-approved for a home loan, once you know what you're capable of, you want as much as you can get for the protection and opportunity it creates. Brandon adds an anecdote about a client who calculated that 41% of his payments in 2025 went to interest — even higher than the 34.5% Nelson cited in the book — reinforcing the idea that redirecting money away from interest into a system you control matters more than obsessing over your insurance rating.

The group discusses why people disqualify themselves too early: confusion over whose life to insure first (self, spouse, or kids), when in almost all cases barring uninsurability the breadwinner's income should be protected first, since every breadwinner wants their income replaced for as long as possible if they were no longer there. Brandon notes that insurance companies view applicants as their "product," carefully underwritten based on decades of actuarial data — and if your health improves (quitting tobacco, losing weight, years cancer-free), insurers will happily re-rate you as a better version of that product. This can motivate people to make health changes, like quitting tobacco once they see the cost difference in black and white.

Nate adds that people often disqualify themselves believing they don't have the money to fund a policy, when in fact repositioning existing income and assets — rather than adding new out-of-pocket cost — frequently makes it possible. Brock emphasizes that this is almost always an "order of operations" problem: for example, someone maxing out a 401(k) while carrying high-interest debt would get a better return by pausing retirement contributions and paying off debt first. He compares it to a chiropractor tracing a knee problem back to a weak core — get to the foundational issue and everything downstream improves. Brock frames money as something that is always flowing somewhere, whether people intend it or not, and repositioning dollars without new out-of-pocket cost is a core principle they try to implement with every client.

They cover "insurable interest" — the financial connection between people that allows one to hold a policy on another, applying to spouses, kids, and in some cases nephews, nieces, grandkids, and business partners. Brock outlines two clear-cut business scenarios: key-person coverage on an employee critical to the business, and buy-sell agreements funded by life insurance so that if a business partner dies, the surviving partner can buy out the deceased's shares rather than end up in business with the partner's spouse. Brock also describes a coal-business client who used to finance a new truck every year and pay it off quickly with cash flow, even though he had the cash on hand — instead, he now buys the truck with a policy loan and repays the loan with the same cash flow the truck generates, recapitalizing his bank.

Nate ties this back to Nelson's point (page 3 of the book) that the book "is not about investments... it's about how one finances the things of life" — the only thing that changes is where you store your wealth as you build it into a policy. The conversation turns to reframing the word "premium": traditionally seen as a pure cost, but once you understand the system, premium becomes an opportunity, especially since cost-basis rules mean the total premiums paid become tax-free withdrawable amounts later in retirement. Brandon shares that he and Nate personally had to work through the tension of resenting premiums in the traditional sense while also wanting to pay as much premium as possible into their own policies — resolving it by recognizing that insurability only decreases with time, so paying premium while you can is a privilege, not just a cost.

Closing out, the hosts pose Nelson's idea that "if nothing changes until your thinking changes, nothing changes," and encourage listeners to ask whether an advisor might see something in their financial situation they can't see themselves. Brandon cites a statistic that 66% of people aren't actively working with any financial advisor, and stresses that he, Nate, and Brock don't charge for an initial conversation — the real cost isn't fees, it's being unwilling to invest in yourself by rethinking how you think about money. They close by inviting listeners to reach out via cashflowlegendz.com or their social channels.

I've had my own practice — I've been a practice owner for 24 years. So, if you're watching, yes, I'm the Doogie Howser of tax, right? I started when I was 10. Now, here's the problem — if you know who Doogie Howser is, you know that I'm lying, right? Because you just brought me back to my childhood, and that was a sweet time when Doogie Howser was on for me. So one of the reasons — to be pretty transparent, I mean I'm blessed to be in the situation that we're in. Most CPAs that own their own firms aren't necessarily living out of their car, we'll say. So the motivation to build this community is because I truly believe everyone can benefit from tax planning and strategy. And I believe that lower to moderate income households can benefit from tax planning and strategy more than high income households. Maybe not dollar-wise. However, an extra $100, $150 in your pocket every month could be a significant portion of their disposable income at that household income level. So, household income level and comfortability with tax planning and strategy are not related. It's just many people in that first category that have never been exposed to tax planning and strategy feel that way because they feel like the dollars aren't big enough.
